lesson: oauthError() logs the whole caught error with console.error. /oauth/register and /oauth/token are unauthenticated and parse request bodies, so V8 JSON SyntaxErrors (which quote the body) and TypeErrors put attacker-controlled text in the server logs. sendChat in apps/web/app/actions/chat.ts:21 does the same with errors that can carry user and model text. Fix: log only the error name or code plus a request id, never e.message or the raw error.

Some writes skip the service pipeline that architecture.md requires for every write (authorize → validate → write → audit → emit). revokeClient cuts access with no audit record at all. issueCode, exchangeToken/mint, revokeToken and the chat.conversation writes are also unaudited. savePolicy writes its own audit but does its permission check outside the pipeline, so callers must remember to check Admin. Fix: move these writes into defineService services, or at least appendAudit for every token issue, rotate and revoke.

baseUrl() falls back to client-supplied x-forwarded-host / x-forwarded-proto / host headers when AMAX_BASE_URL is unset. Those values become the OAuth issuer, the authorization_servers list, the token audience and the expected audience in /api/mcp, so the audience binding is meaningless and the metadata can be poisoned. Fix: require AMAX_BASE_URL in production (fail at boot), or validate the host against an allowlist.

blockedReason() treats an unset region as compliant: `r && r !== p.dataRegion` skips null entries. A tenant that sets a data region but leaves where AI, the database or files run unknown gets AI turned on, and the page says "Database, files and AI in region". The comparison is also an exact, case-sensitive string compare of free text. Fix: when dataRegion is set, block if any region is unset, and normalise regions to a fixed list of codes.

Redaction and the untrusted-data rules (033 AC-2/AC-3) cover only `record` DataItems. Chat pins are sent as `text: JSON.stringify(record)` (packages/chat/src/engine.ts:70), so classified fields the tenant blocks go out unredacted. Every tool_result is sent to the model raw: not passed through redactRecord, not wrapped by quoteData, and not checked by looksLikeInjection. Fix: send pins as records with their sensitivity map, and run tool results through the same redaction, quoting and injection flagging.

ai.call records neither the policy_version used for the redaction and block decision nor the model id the provider actually returned (r.model). It logs the configured alias `m` instead. Fix: add a policy_version column and store result.model.

costOf() returns 0 for any model missing from PRICES. AMAX_AI_MODEL can be overridden, and providers return dated model ids, so an unknown price shows as "$0.00" rather than "unknown". Fix: return null for unknown models and show the cost as unknown, or reject unpriced models at boot.

confirmAction reads `pending`, runs the write, and only then saves the shortened list, with no lock or atomic claim. Two concurrent confirms both run the write. The "Add it" button is not disabled while the request is in flight, and the 'no longer pending' test is single-session. Fix: claim the action atomically first, e.g. `update chat.conversation set pending = pending - <idx> where id=$1 and pending @> [{id}] returning`, and add a two-worker race test.

createProposal picks the next key with max()+1 and then inserts, with no lock. Concurrent creates on the same project compute the same key, and one fails with a raw unique-violation error. Fix: lock the project row (`select ... for update`) or keep a per-project counter, and add a two-session race test.

installAuthorizer now uses canEver(), so the pipeline's authorize step passes on any qualified grant (@managed, @assigned, @own) without a record. This widens every existing defineService in the repo: any service that relied on authorize() for scoped grants and never calls assertCan with the record now allows all records. Fix: keep can() as the default and opt in per service (e.g. a `scoped: true` flag that forces a record check), or check that every scoped action's service calls assertCan.

managedProjectIds is documented as what "feeds the viewer's @managed scope", but nothing in the diff wires it into loadViewer, viewerForUser or authenticateMcp. Every test plants managedProjects on the viewer by hand (`{ ...v, managedProjects: ... }`), which does not drive the real path. In the app, a PM who is not an Admin has empty managedProjects, so every @managed delivery grant fails. Fix: resolve managed and assigned projects through a registered resolver at viewer load, and test through loadViewer.

ReleaseMap still takes its columns from releases[0].stages. 042 made environments per project, and the table was changed to use the union of environments, but the map was not. Rows from projects with different or reordered environments are drawn against another project's columns (lastI indexes the row's own stages). Fix: lay out by environment name or position, using the same union as the table.

`can(viewer, "delivery:deployment:record", {})` has no projectId, and the button is shown whenever a release has a deployment or no proposals. Users without the permission (Finance, Leadership, or a PM on another project) get Promote and Retry buttons that throw an unhandled forbidden error. The service does refuse the write, so this is wrong behaviour, not a bypass. Fix: add projectId to ReleaseRow, check `can(..., { projectId })`, and hide the form when the check fails.

syncProposal upserts with `on conflict (tenant_id,key)` but does not check that the existing row is a specclaw row. syncSpecclaw only treats rows with source='specclaw' as existing. A proposal created by hand in AMX (key AMX-041) is overwritten when specclaw change 041 appears, and is counted as 'created'. Its source stays null, so every later run rewrites and re-audits it, which breaks "an unchanged re-sync writes nothing". Fix: refuse or skip on a key collision with a non-specclaw row, or set source and project on conflict.

json() returns {} on a parse failure, so a corrupt state.json looks the same as a missing one. The phases are lost and the change drops back a phase, and the sync records that as a real phase change. Fix: throw, or mark the record as unreadable and skip it.

meta.sha records only main's GITHUB_SHA, but the phase and tasks can come from overlay branches (specclaw/*) at commits that are not recorded. bin.ts also defaults --sha to 'unknown'. Fix: record the source ref and commit per record (e.g. `specclaw/040@<sha>`), and make --sha required.

Each row is one client plus one person, but its Revoke button posts only clientId. revokeClient then revokes that client's tokens for every user in the tenant. Fix: send the user id and revoke `where client_id = $1 and user_id = $2`.

Voice uses window.SpeechRecognition/webkitSpeechRecognition. In Chrome this sends the audio to the browser vendor's cloud, yet the policy screen says "processed by the browser". Voice is not gated by blockedReason or the data-region check, and the vendor is missing from the Subprocessors card. Fix: gate voice on the region and ZDR checks, and name the browser vendor as a subprocessor (or use on-device recognition only).

module-standard ✓auto: "every personal-data table has a 032 retention entry in the manifest". delivery.project.manager_name, delivery.proposal.owner_name and delivery.deployment.recorded_by/voided_by store person names, but the manifest declares no retention rules. Fix: add retention entries for these tables.

voidDeployment takes a release's proposals out of Released whenever the release has no live deployment to an environment that is Prod right now. It does this even when the voided record is not a Prod deployment, and even when Prod has since been moved to another environment or switched off. Only un-release when the voided row was a 'deployed' row on the environment that released the proposals. Add a variant test covering: a Dev void after Prod is unmarked, a Dev void after Prod moved, and a real Prod void.

setReleaseProposals (and the same loop in createRelease, line 113) runs `update ... set release_id` on any key in the project, including proposals already released through another release. That rewrites shipped history. Exclude `phase = 'released'` rows, or reject them, in both copies.

The rule that assigns proposals to a release is written twice, and the copies disagree. setReleaseProposals throws on an unknown key; createRelease silently skips it. Put both on one helper that throws.

The built-in search swallows every module error (`.catch(() => [])`), so a DB failure or timeout looks exactly like 'no matches'. Catch only ForbiddenError and ScopeError; surface any other error, or mark that module as not searched.

Withdrawn spec proposals keep their phase, so phaseCounts, the board lanes and the proposal list still count them as in flight. Exclude `meta->>'withdrawn'` rows from the counts and lanes, or show them separately.

Overlay branches feed persisted phases, but only main's sha is recorded (`--sha`). The commit each specclaw/* overlay was read at is never stored, so a phase cannot be traced to its source. Record each overlay's commit, for example in meta per record. A branch with no .specclaw also makes `git archive` fail, which aborts the whole sync.

The corrupt-state fix only covers a corrupt state.json on main. When an overlay's state.json is corrupt, take() returns early because main's copy is readable (`if (r.unreadable && cur && !cur.unreadable) return;`). The overlay is dropped without any report and the record keeps main's earlier phase. That is the same 'drops back a phase' defect, reached through a different source. Fix: when an overlay that would replace the record is unreadable, mark the merged record unreadable (keep its source) so syncSpecclaw skips and reports it. Add a test for the overlay case next to the main case.

blockedReason() now calls normalizeRegion() on stored values, and normalizeRegion throws on anything outside the closed list. Before this change the screen saved regions as free text (placeholder 'e.g. Australia'), and no migration normalises existing ai.settings rows. A legacy value therefore turns blockedReason into an exception rather than a reason. The AI settings page, voiceAllowed and voiceEnabled() in apps/web/lib/server.ts all throw, so the Admin can't open the screen to fix the value. prepare() throws a plain Error instead of AiDisabledError. Fix: add a migration that normalises or clears unknown stored regions. Inside blockedReason, treat an unparsable region as a block reason ('region X is not recognised'), not an exception.

The atomic claim only guards confirm against confirm (and cancel). chatTurn still loads the conversation, runs the model (seconds long), then saves the whole convo, pending list included, with save(). A confirm that claims an action during that window is undone when chatTurn writes back its stale pending list, so the card can be confirmed again and the write runs twice. Fix: have chatTurn change pending only through atomic jsonb operations (append its new actions, never rewrite the whole list), or take the same row lock across the turn's read-modify-write. Add a race test where a confirm and a chatTurn run on one conversation.

Round 1 required every tool_result to be redacted, quoted and checked for injection. Only the success path does this. When a tool throws, its error message goes to the model raw (`content: e.message`): it isn't wrapped by quoteData, isn't checked by looksLikeInjection, and doesn't set p.injection. Tool and DB errors can echo record values or attacker-supplied text. Fix: send a fixed or quoted error string. Run the message through looksLikeInjection, and set p.injection when it matches.

The ReleaseMap fix handles projects with different environments but not reordered ones, although the finding named both. stageColumns orders the union by the first position seen, so a project whose own order differs is drawn against columns in a different order. lastI then points at a column to the left of stages the release has already reached. Fix: draw each row's stations in its own stage order (by s.position), or build the column order so it is consistent with every project's order. Add a test with two projects that order the same environments differently.

Refresh-token reuse detection (revoke the whole grant, audit reuse_detected) has no test that drives it. The e2e only checks that the replay returns 400, which also passed before this change. Nothing checks that the rotated access/refresh pair is revoked after a replay. The fix also depends on auth.lookup_refresh still returning rows whose revoked_at is set. That is why rotation stopped nulling refresh_hash, and if the function filters out revoked rows the whole branch never runs. Fix: add a test: rotate, replay the old refresh token, then assert the new access token gets 401 and the new refresh token is refused, and that an auth.oauth.reuse_detected audit row exists.

desired() now puts `source: r.source` into meta, and in production that value contains the main sha (`main@<sha>`). The fingerprint comment says the commit sha must not count as a change, but `source` carries the sha under another name. Unless fingerprint drops meta.source as well as meta.sha, every sync at a new commit marks every record changed, rewrites it and audits it. That breaks 'an unchanged re-sync writes nothing'. The new test can't catch this: it calls readSpecclaw(repo2) with a plain path, so the ref stays the same between runs. Fix: leave the sha part of source out of the fingerprint (compare only the branch name), and test two runs at different `main@sha` refs with no spec change.

Errors are told apart by the string `e?.name === "ForbiddenError" | "ScopeError"`. If either class does not set `this.name`, its name is 'Error', so an expected permission refusal is reported as a module outage. Renaming or minifying a class has the same effect. Also, no test covers 'DB error → notSearched' or 'forbidden → silently empty'. Fix: use `instanceof ForbiddenError || instanceof ScopeError`, and add a variant test with a throwing module, a forbidden module and a working one.

Round 1 asked for every tool_result to be redacted, quoted and checked for injection. The error path now quotes the message and checks it for injection, but it never redacts it. The success path is redacted ('tool results and nested data are redacted and quoted'), and the stated reason for this fix is that errors 'can echo record values'. Quoting a value doesn't hide it, so classified data in a DB or tool error still reaches the provider. Fix: run the error text through the same redaction as results. Better still, send a fixed string ('read_ticket failed', plus a logError reference) and keep the raw message server-side. Add a test where the error message contains a classified value or an email address.

The fix for reordered environments only works when the projects' orders don't contradict each other. When they do (a cycle), stageColumns falls back to position/name order, and ReleaseMap still assumes 'columns agree with it'. lastI = max column index of reached stages, so the line is drawn past columns the project hasn't reached, while `back` is read from the last stage in the project's own order. The round-1 finding offered drawing each row by its own s.position as the alternative, and that handles this case. The only contradiction test checks that each name appears once, not what gets drawn. Fix: in ReleaseMap, place each row's stations and line by its own stage order (or flag rows whose order disagrees with the columns). Add a test with two projects that order the same environments in opposite ways and check the drawn extent.

This adds a project row lock to syncProposal and claims it makes sync and createProposal safe together ('keys share one namespace'). No test runs a syncProposal and a createProposal at the same time on one project. The existing race test only runs concurrent createProposal calls, so it stays green if this new lock is deleted. Fix: add a race test with two real sessions, one syncing a specclaw key and one creating a proposal in the same project, and assert the keys are distinct and nothing is lost.

The proposal retention clock starts only at `delivery.proposal.released`. A proposal that is never released keeps `owner_name` with no end date: one withdrawn by sync, one cancelled, or one still open on an abandoned project. The project entry has the same gap: the clock starts at `delivery.project.closed`, so a project that is abandoned and never formally closed keeps `manager_name` forever. The fix covers the happy path, not every way a record can end. Fix: start the clock at the record's terminal state, whichever comes first (released or withdrawn, closed or archived), or add a fallback start such as last update. Also check at manifest load that every `start` names an event the module actually emits (`start` is a free string today).

The new comment says the error message 'stays out of the prompt and the log, which keeps a reference only'. But the whole error object `e` is passed to `logError(`ai.tool ${call.name}`, e)`, and a logError helper normally records the error's message and stack. The new test's own example ('gross 285000 for kasun@lumenlabs.test') would then be written to the server log, so classified pay data and an email address end up in logs. No test checks what gets logged. Fix: log only the error kind or name plus the reference, or redact before logging. Then add an assertion that the logged output contains neither '285000' nor 'kasun@'.

The new KeyTakenError skip path in syncSpecclaw has no test that is sure to reach it. The race test checks skipped entries only in `for (const s of sync.skipped)`, which passes without checking anything when no collision happens. The test also never requires at least one collision. If the sync wins every key, the KeyTakenError catch never runs, so a regression goes unnoticed. That includes defineService wrapping the error so `instanceof KeyTakenError` fails and the whole sync aborts. Fix: add a test that always collides. Create a proposal by hand that takes a specclaw key, run the sync through the real path, and assert that `skipped` contains that key and that the other records still sync.

The round-2 finding asked for a test showing 'distinct keys and nothing lost'. The fix instead accepts a lost record: when a hand-made create takes a key that a specclaw folder maps to, that folder is skipped. Nothing ever gets it back, so every later sync skips it again and the spec change never appears in delivery. The test writes this in as expected (`synced.length + sync.skipped.length === 6`). The cause is that hand-made and synced keys share one numbering. The collision is now reported, but the record is still lost. Fix: give synced and hand-made proposals keys that can't collide (a separate prefix or range, or a hand-made create that skips numbers specclaw has reserved), or reassign the hand-made key. Assert that all 6 specclaw records sync.

NotPendingError is thrown for anything that is no longer pending: already confirmed, already cancelled, or (since claim() returns null) an action id that doesn't exist or isn't the caller's. The page treats all of these as `handled` and moves the card to the 'done' state. It also tells the user to 'Check the record' when no record may exist. Fix: have claim() or NotPendingError carry the final state (confirmed or cancelled). Show 'done' only for confirmed and 'cancelled' for cancelled, and keep unknown ids as an error.

The proposal retention clock now starts on `delivery.release.deployed`. That event's subject is a release, not a proposal row, and RetentionEntry has no way to say how an event maps to rows of `delivery.proposal`. The new defineModule check only confirms that the module emits the event, not that the event is about that table. The comment says the clock starts 'when a proposal's release reaches Prod', but nothing limits the event to Prod deployments, and the start isn't undone when the releasing deployment is voided. Fix: start on a proposal-level event (for example the phase change to released, which phaseEvent already emits per proposal), or add a declared subject or key mapping to `start`. Then check at load that the event's subject is the retained table.

Round-4 B1 finding: this is an instance fix. Starting hand-made numbers at 1001 only protects projects that already have a specclaw row. Three cases still collide and lose a spec change on every sync. (1) Proposals made by hand before the first sync. The new LG test writes this in as expected: `skipped: ["LG-001…"]`. (2) Hand-made proposals created under the old numbering in projects that are already synced, such as an existing RB-002. Nothing renumbers them. (3) Spec changes numbered 1000 or higher, which share the hand-made range (change 1001 and hand-made RB-1001). The finding asked that all spec records sync. Fix: give the two kinds keys that can't collide, for example a separate prefix for hand-made keys. Alternatively, migrate or reassign hand-made keys that sit on spec numbers when a project is first synced. Add a test where a pre-existing hand-made LG-001 and spec 001 both end up present.

The fix tells a retried confirm what happened the first time, but the cancel path does not. cancelAction swallows every NotPendingError, including `decision: "confirmed"`. cancelChat then returns normally and Chat.tsx shows 'Cancelled. Nothing was changed.' even though the write ran. An unknown action id is also reported as a successful cancel. Fix: when the decision is not 'cancelled', rethrow from cancelAction, or return the decision. Show 'already done' for 'confirmed' and an error for null, and test both cases.

claim() records `decided = confirmed` before registry.call runs, and removes it only if the call fails. While the write is still running, a second confirm reads 'confirmed' and gets 'This was already done.' If the write then fails, the card goes back to pending and nothing was done. An in-flight write is reported as done. Fix: record 'confirmed' only after the call succeeds, and treat a claim in progress as its own state ('in progress', not 'done').

Round-4 B3 finding asked that unknown ids stay an error. confirmChat now returns a plain error for them, but the UI still puts every non-ok result that isn't 'confirmed' into the 'cancelled' state. That covers an unknown action id, 'conversation not found', and a tool failure where the engine puts the card back in pending. Each one is drawn as a closed, cancelled card with no buttons. Fix: show 'cancelled' only when `r.earlier === "cancelled"`. Show other errors as an error state and keep the retry buttons when the server restored the card.

The comment says every path that closes a project records closed_at. Two paths don't. The trigger fires only on `UPDATE OF status`, so a project inserted as closed (fixtures, imports) gets closed_at null. The migration also doesn't backfill projects that are already closed. In both cases the project retention entry (`start: { at: ["closed_at"] }`, no idle) never starts, and manager names are kept forever. Fix: make the trigger `before insert or update of status`, and backfill closed_at for existing closed rows (for example from updated_at). Test the insert path and an existing closed row.

"confirming" has no way to end except the success path or the catch around registry.call. Two cases leave it stuck. (a) The process dies after claim(), for example on a serverless timeout or redeploy. (b) registry.call succeeds but the later `decided || {actionId: confirmed}` update fails. That error is not an ActionFailedError, so confirmChat shows a generic error even though the write ran. In both cases decided stays "confirming" forever, the card is no longer in pending, and every later confirm or cancel answers "This is being done right now." A state of unknown is reported as in progress, and nothing ever resolves it. Fix: store a timestamp with the claim and report a claim older than the call's timeout as unknown, not as working. Also record the decision in the same transaction as the write, or retry it. Test the stale-claim path.

The rekey writes to the hand-made proposal (found.id) inside the sync service. The only audit record is `after.rekeyed` on the spec row's resourceId. No audit row is written for the moved proposal's own resourceId, and no event is emitted. The module standard requires every write to be audited and to emit its events. Anything that took the key from earlier events, notes, chat transcripts or other modules now finds the spec change under 'LG-001' instead of the hand-made proposal. The rekey also moves released hand-made proposals, which renames shipped history. Fix: audit the rekey as its own write with resourceId = found.id, and emit a `delivery.proposal.rekeyed` event (from, to, id) in contracts. Decide on released rows explicitly (refuse or flag), and test both.

The round-4 finding named three collision variants. The tests cover only two: hand-made keys in an already-synced project (now H series) and a hand-made LG-001 made before the first sync. Two variants are untested. (2) A hand-made proposal created under an older numbering in a project that is already synced, such as RB-002 or a round-4 RB-1001, whose spec change arrives later. Depending on how syncSpecclaw computes `cur`, a key previously skipped may never reach syncProposal. (3) A spec change numbered 1000 or higher, like 1001. Add a table-driven case for each that asserts both rows are present and that the hand-made row is rekeyed.

The round-4/5 UI defect was the mapping from a server result to the card's state. The engine test checks the decisions it throws, but nothing tests outcomeOf, confirmChat/cancelChat or Chat.tsx `apply`. If the mapping regressed, for example by sending NotPendingError(null) to 'cancelled', every test would still pass. Add a table-driven test over outcomeOf: ActionFailedError → open, confirmed → done, confirming → working, cancelled → cancelled, null → error, other Error → error.

This fixes only the named case. The decision is not recorded in the same transaction as the write. registry.call(viewer, …) gets no `tx`, so the service commits on its own connection, and close() then runs in the outer transaction that decide() still holds. Two cases are still open. (a) The outer transaction fails or the process dies after registry.call commits. (b) registry.call throws after its commit, for example when the commit ack is lost or the connection resets. In both cases the card goes back to pending and reads as 'nothing changed', so the next confirm runs the write again. Round 5 ended in a stuck 'confirming'; this ends in a duplicate write. permanent() also treats every unrecognised error as retryable, and the new test uses exactly that ambiguous case ('connection reset') as its 'safe to retry' example. A second problem: each confirm now holds one pooled connection, locked, while the service opens a second. With a pool of 1 (common on serverless), or N confirms at once on a pool of N, it deadlocks. Fix: pass `tx` into registry.call so the service write and close() commit together, or make the write idempotent on actionId (store actionId with the created row and look it up before running again). Add a test that kills the outer transaction after registry.call commits, then retries and asserts exactly one row.

Round 6 asked for two variants. Variant 2 (an older numbering such as a round-4 RB-1001) and variant 3 (a spec change ≥1000) were each supposed to assert that both rows survive and the hand-made row is rekeyed. The new table only ever plants a hand-made row on `${P}-002`. The 1001 spec folder syncs onto a free key, so a hand-made `${P}-1001` from round-4 numbering, colliding with spec change 1001, is never tested. That is the one collision the ≥1000 change makes newly reachable. Add a row to the table: hand-made `${P}-1001` exists, spec 1001-big arrives, and the test asserts it was rekeyed to H-series and both rows are present.

This is an instance fix for the duplicate-write class. A retry now checks the stored result only inside the service transaction, and it does so after authorize() and safeParse() have run again. Any step before that check can fail on the retry: authorize, validate, or a registry or tool pre-check before the service. That failure then closes the card as `failed`, and the user is told "This couldn't be done… Nothing was changed" even though the write committed on the first attempt. Fix: look the key up first. Do it at the top of `call` before authorize, or in confirmAction before registry.call. Return the stored outcome if there is one. Add a variant test where the retry hits a refusal after a committed first attempt.

retryable() replaced the PERMANENT set, but it only covers error classes that were given `retryable = false` in this diff. The old checks are gone. ZodError was in the set, and so was any error carrying code 'forbidden', 'invalid_input' or 'not_found' that is not a ToolError. Both are now treated as retryable. A permanent failure therefore leaves the card open with "Try again or cancel" for good. Fix: keep the code/name checks, or mark every permanent error class, and extend the chat outcome test table with ZodError and code-only errors.

Nothing checks that the idempotency key was actually used. withIdempotency covers only the first defineService call in the scope. If a tool writes outside defineService, or makes a second service call after the first, the later writes are not covered by the key. confirmAction still reports such a retry as safe (retry:true), and a cancel 'wins' while the write still runs. Fix: return the scope's `used` flag from withIdempotency (or check it afterwards). If the key was never taken, or the tool made more than one write, fail closed: treat the outcome as unknown and do not offer a blind retry.

The 'Cancel wins' race holds the confirm at a gate before registry.call, so the cancel commits before the service transaction even begins. The claimed guarantee that a cancel and a confirm can't both win depends on cancel's claimKey blocking on the confirm's uncommitted key row. No test ever has the cancel arrive while the write transaction is open. Fix: put the gate inside spec.run (after claimKey, before commit), start cancelAction, release the gate, and assert three things: the cancel throws NotPendingError('confirmed'), exactly one row exists, and the card is recorded as confirmed.

settleKey stores the service's raw `out.result` in core.idempotency. The audit row goes through redact() by sensitivity class; this copy skips that. The table has no retention rule, and amax_app has no delete grant, so rows can never be pruned. Any personal or sensitive fields in a write result (pay, health, bank, candidate) are copied unredacted into a core table and kept forever, against the 002/032 classification and retention requirement. Fix: store only what a replay needs (for example ids or keys) or redact by spec.sensitive. Add a TTL or retention job and the delete grant it needs.

The exactly-once and cancel-wins guarantee only holds if the tool's first defineService call is the write, and if the tool makes no other write. Nothing checks this. Case 1: a write tool that calls no defineService at all (for example the packages/mcp admin writes that skip the pipeline) never takes the key. Then a cancel claims the key, the confirm still writes, and settle() quietly returns because the card is no longer pending. confirmAction then returns success, so the UI says 'done' while the conversation records 'cancelled'. Case 2: a tool whose first service call is a read, or a tool that makes two writes. The key goes to the first call only. On a retry, every other write runs again. Fix: give withIdempotency a way to report whether the key was taken, and have confirmAction fail closed (ActionFailedError, not done) when registry.call returns without using it. Either reject chat write tools that make more than one write, or give each nested write its own derived key. When settle() finds the card already cancelled after a write committed, record it as confirmed, not as nothing.

The old permanent() list was replaced with a `retryable === false` flag on selected classes. Two variants the old code covered are dropped. (1) ZodError was in PERMANENT but has no flag, so it now counts as retryable. (2) The old check also read a `code` of forbidden, invalid_input or not_found on any error, and only ToolError got the flag. retryable() also looks only at the top-level error, so a permanent error wrapped as `cause` reads as retryable. Each of these leaves the card open with 'Try again' forever, when it should close as failed. Fix: keep a single classifier that covers the names, the code values and the cause chain. Add a table test with ZodError, an error carrying a code, and a wrapped ForbiddenError.

The fail-closed check for a tool that made no service write only covers the success path (`run.ok && run.writes === 0`). On the error path a tool with writes === 0 goes to lookupKey, finds nothing, and then retryable() decides. A tool that wrote around the pipeline and then threw a transient error is offered a blind retry, and the write repeats. This is the 'key never taken' variant from round 8, fixed only for one branch. Fix: the error path should only offer `retry` when writes === 1 and the key has no stored outcome. When writes === 0, close as `unknown` unless the tool provably wrote nothing. Better: reject chat write tools that are not pipeline writes when they are registered. Add raw_write-then-throw to the it.each table.

Case 1 of the round-8 finding was fixed only on the confirm side. A tool that writes around defineService never claims the key, so cancelAction can still claim it as cancelled and settle the card 'cancelled' while the raw write runs. The confirm then reports 'unknown', but settleNow(unknown) is a no-op on a card that is already cancelled. The conversation record and the cancelling user's UI still say 'Cancelled. Nothing was changed.' even though a row was written. The new tests never run a cancel against raw_write. Fix: refuse to create chat cards for write tools that don't go through the keyed pipeline. Or, when confirm ends 'unknown' or 'confirmed' after a cancel claimed the key, overwrite the cancelled decision with 'unknown'. Add a race test for raw_write against cancel.

pruneKeysJob deletes replay records by age alone. A record is the only proof that a card's write committed when the process died between the service commit and settleNow, which leaves the card pending. Nothing expires or settles such cards. Once the record is pruned, confirmAction's lookupKey returns null and the write runs again. Fix: only prune keys whose card is decided. Or make confirmAction refuse cards older than KEY_DAYS and close them as 'unknown'. Or settle the pending card from the record before deleting it. Add a test: committed write, settle skipped, record aged past KEY_DAYS and pruned, then confirm → must not write.

The round-8 fix for 'raw write result persisted unredacted' (B8) fixed only the core.idempotency copy. The new done() helper still writes `JSON.stringify(result)`, the service's full raw result, into the conversation message stored in chat.conversation. That copy skips spec.sensitive redaction and the 032 retention rule in the same way. The text is also fed back to the model on later turns. Fix: record only the Replay shape (resource id and key), or redact the result by the service's sensitivity map, before writing it to the conversation.

takeIdempotencyKey counts every defineService call made anywhere under the async scope, including ones nested inside the keyed service's own run(). The architecture sanctions cross-module writes through the owning module's contract command functions (for example hr.contracts.createPersonFromHire), and those run the owner's defineService. A single logical write that uses a command therefore always shows writes=2, and confirmAction closes it as 'unknown' after it succeeded. The nested write also runs in its own transaction, outside the key, so the outer key does not really cover it. Fix: decide the contract for nested service calls explicitly. Either give the nested write a key derived from the outer one (and do not count it as a second top-level write), or reject keyed tools that use commands, and document the choice in the idempotency contract. Add a test with a service that calls another service from its run().

`expired()` only expires a card when it has a usable `createdAt`. `Boolean(a.createdAt) && …` means a card with no `createdAt` never expires. This covers every card stored before this change, since `createdAt` is optional on `PendingAction`. A malformed value also never expires: `Date.parse` returns NaN, and `NaN > x` is false. Those cards are exactly the ones whose replay records `pruneKeysJob` can delete by age, so the round-9 prune finding is fixed only for new cards. Fix: fail closed. Treat a missing or unparsable `createdAt` as expired (or as unknown). Alternatively, backfill `createdAt` for existing pending cards in a migration and make the field required.

After the record is pruned, an expired card is settled as 'expired' with the note `The request … expired before it was confirmed`. The UI (chat-outcome.ts) tells the user 'Ask again if you still want it.' Once the record is gone, the engine can't tell 'never confirmed' from 'confirmed, committed, settle lost'. Those are the two cases the round-9 finding was about. This reports 'could not know' as 'nothing happened' and asks the user to repeat the write. Fix: when a card is expired and has no record, settle it as 'unknown' (or as an expired decision whose note says to check the record before asking again). Don't claim it expired before it was confirmed.

The test for the prune fix uses one fresh card with no previous attempt. It never runs the scenario named in the finding: committed write, settle skipped, record aged past KEY_DAYS and pruned through the real `pruneKeysJob`, then confirm must not write. It also has no variant table. These variants are missing: a card without `createdAt`, a card with a malformed `createdAt`, and cancel after prune. Fix: make it an `it.each` over these variants, drive the prune through `pruneKeysJob`, and assert that no second row is written and the decision is not 'never done'.

Raw error messages still reach the model through two paths that the round 2-4 toolFailure fix and the round 9 doneNote fix do not cover. (1) When a pinned record fails to load, the code sends `{ error: e.message }` as the record. redactDeep cannot redact that string, so it is quoted to the model as data. (2) The confirmAction 'failed' path (~line 211) writes `couldn't be done: ${message}` into the conversation messages, and the model reads those back on the next turn. Fix: build both from the error kind plus a logError reference, as toolFailure does. Add a table-driven test covering pin errors and failed-confirm notes.

Environment names are matched two ways. recordDeployment and voidDeployment use lower(name) = lower(input). upsertEnvironment and removeEnvironment use exact `name = input.name`, and the unique constraint (project_id, name) is case-sensitive. So 'Prod' and 'prod' can both exist, upsert creates a second environment instead of matching the existing one, and the case-insensitive lookups then pick an arbitrary row. The ReleaseDeployed event also carries the caller's spelling (input.environment) instead of env.name. Fix: use one matcher for every service (for example a unique index on (project_id, lower(name)) plus lower() everywhere), and emit env.name.

Each history row has its own Void form, but it sends only the environment name. voidDeployment always voids the latest non-voided deployment for that environment, so Void on an older row voids a different record. Fix: send the deployment id and void by id, checking that it belongs to the release.

nextStep finds the next stage by `position === last.position + 1` and treats 'no next stage' as Live. Positions are not renumbered when an environment is removed, so a gap ends the chain early. A release whose last reached stage is not a deployed Prod (Prod status 'testing', or a project with no Prod) also shows 'Live'. Fix: take the next stage in sort order, and return null only when a Prod deployment has status 'deployed'.

Retention for delivery.deployment starts the clock for both recorded_by and voided_by at the deployment's `at`. voided_by is set when the record is voided, possibly years later, so the voider's name is anonymised less than seven years after the void. The round-4 fix covered closed_at for projects but not this field. Fix: give voided_by its own entry with start.at ['voided_at'].

Route params are decoded twice. The comment says Next already hands over decoded segments, and matchRoute runs decodeURIComponent on them again. Fix: drop the second decode, or decode in exactly one place.

A pinned record whose read fails is sent to the model as `{ error: e.message }`. Round 3 fixed this for tool calls: converse() gives the model a fixed phrase per error kind (toolFailure) and never the message, because messages can echo classified values and attacker text. The pin path, a second way data reaches the provider, skips that fix. Fix: on failure, use toolFailure(pin.tool, e, logError(...)) or a fixed marker, never e.message.

Un-releasing always sets proposals to 'verified', whatever phase they had before the Prod deployment. That phase is never recorded, so voiding a mistaken deployment cannot undo it. Fix: store each proposal's phase before release (on the proposal or the releasing deployment) and restore it on void, with the from/to events matching.

A specclaw-synced proposal's phase has two writers. syncProposal overwrites phase from the repo, and recordDeployment (Prod) and moveProposal (MCP/chat; only the board UI hides Move for specclaw rows) also write it. The next sync sees a fingerprint mismatch and silently reverts, emitting a backwards phase_changed. Fix: pick one owner. Either recordDeployment and moveProposal refuse or skip source='specclaw' rows, or the sync keeps a 'released' set by a Prod deployment.

assignProposals only checks 'already shipped in another release'. It does not check whether the target release already has a live Prod deployment. A proposal added to a release that is already live never becomes released, which breaks 'Released means it reached Prod' for that release. Fix: refuse to add proposals to a release with a live released deployment, or release them in the same write.

The data-region gate trusts regions.ai, an Admin-typed declaration. providerRegion and aiRegion never reach anthropicProvider, which always calls the SDK's default endpoint. So 'AI runs in AU' unblocks AI without anything making calls stay in AU. Fix: make the provider endpoint/region come from the policy (or the deployment config), and block when the configured endpoint's region is unknown or doesn't match.

When deploymentId is given, voidDeployment uses it alone and ignores input.environment, which is still required. It only checks that the id belongs to the release. The environment the caller named is never checked against the record. void_deployment is a destructive MCP/chat tool, so a mismatched pair voids a record in a different environment without warning. That includes the releasing Prod record, which un-releases proposals. Fix: when deploymentId is given, also require the record's environment to match lower(input.environment), or refuse the call; then add a mismatch case to the void-by-id test.

The migration creates the unique index on (project_id, lower(name)) without first resolving existing case-duplicates. Before this round, upsertEnvironment matched names exactly, so it could create them. On any database that already has 'Prod' and 'prod' in one project, the migration fails and blocks the deploy. Fix: merge or rename the duplicates first, moving deployments to the kept row, then create the index. Add a migration test that seeds a duplicate.

nextStep returns 'No Prod stage' whenever the furthest reached stage has nothing after it in order, even when the project has a Prod stage that was never deployed. upsertEnvironment appends new environments after Prod (max(position)+1), and recordDeployment accepts any environment. So a release that reached a stage placed after Prod shows 'No Prod stage' and offers no way to deploy to Prod. Fix: return 'No Prod stage' only when no stage has isProd. Otherwise, when nothing follows the last reached stage, offer the first Prod stage that isn't deployed. Add this case to the table test.

assignProposals counts live Prod deployments once, at the start, with no lock on the release. recordDeployment (Prod) can commit between that count and the release_id updates. It releases only the proposals it saw, and the newly assigned one stays in a live release that it never shipped with. That is the same 'live release with an unreleased proposal' outcome this fix is meant to prevent. Fix: lock the release row (select … for update) in both assignProposals and recordDeployment before checking or releasing. Add a two-session race test.

The fix for migration 0008 has one test, and it covers one variant: a single non-Prod duplicate with one deployment. The migration has three behaviours that the test never runs. First, it keeps is_prod when the duplicate that gets deleted was the Prod row. Second, it merges three or more rows that differ only by case. Third, it leaves projects with no duplicates untouched. If the `update ... set is_prod = true` line were deleted, this test would still pass. Fix: make it a table-driven test over at least these cases: a duplicate that is Prod while the kept row is not; three case variants, each with deployments; and a project with no duplicates. Each case should check the kept row, the is_prod flag and where the deployments ended up.

The race test only covers the recordDeployment side of the fix. It holds a FOR KEY SHARE lock from a raw owner session and checks that recordDeployment waits. It never runs the race the finding named: setReleaseProposals/assignProposals in one session and a Prod recordDeployment in another. So the lock on the assign side is untested. If setReleaseProposals stops calling releaseOf, or reads the release with a plain select before releaseOf, this test stays green and the 'live release with an unreleased proposal' race comes back. Fix: open two real service calls. Start setReleaseProposals (adding a proposal) on a release in session A and hold it before commit. In session B run recordDeployment(Prod). Assert that the proposal is either released or the assignment is refused, never assigned and left unreleased. Run the same race in the other order too.

Instance fix of the round-14 B7 finding. The new race test starts setReleaseProposals and recordDeployment together with Promise.allSettled and hopes they overlap. Nothing holds session A before it commits, which is what the finding asked for. Reversing the array only changes which call starts first, and both still run unsynchronised. Whether the two transactions ever overlap inside the window between reading the release and writing is left to timing. This means the test does not reliably fail when releaseOf's `for update` is removed from either side. The it.each lock test above only shows that each call waits on an outside key-share lock; it never runs the two services against each other. Fix: hold setReleaseProposals inside its transaction after releaseOf, for example with a test hook or a gate in a wrapped tx. Then start recordDeployment(Prod) in a second session and assert it is still pending. Release the gate and assert the proposal ends up released. Repeat with recordDeployment held, and assert that setReleaseProposals is refused with the live-release error.

The race assertion treats every outcome where the proposal is not assigned as 'refused'. Promise.allSettled swallows every rejection, so a call that failed for an unrelated reason passes the same way: a forbidden error, a deadlock, a serialization error, a bad key, or a crash. Since 'could not run' reads as 'correctly refused', the assertion can't tell the guard working from the code being broken. Fix: inspect the settled results. When the proposal is unassigned, require that setReleaseProposals rejected with /already live in Prod/ and that recordDeployment fulfilled. When it is assigned, require that both calls fulfilled.

This diff deletes the deterministic test 'a release already live in Prod takes no new proposals; keeping its own is fine'. That test checked the refusal message (`already live in Prod; put LIV-002 in a new release`) and checked that re-saving the release's own proposals is still allowed. The race test that replaces it does neither: it never checks the error text, and it never calls setReleaseProposals with the existing set after the release is live. The guard for the earlier major is now covered only by a timing-dependent test. Fix: restore the deleted test next to the new ones.

This only fixes one instance of the race. The round-14 finding named two ways to add a proposal to a release that can race a Prod deployment: setReleaseProposals and assignProposals. The new deterministic race table only covers setReleaseProposals against recordDeployment. assignProposals (adding from the proposal side) is never held against a Prod recordDeployment, in either order. So if its `for update` on the release is removed or missing, no test fails. Fix: add the assignProposals path to the it.each table, in both orders (assign-first: ends released; deploy-first: refused with /already live in Prod/). Use the same holdAfterReleaseLock gate.

This is an instance fix of the round-16 finding. The finding asked for the assignProposals path to be raced against a Prod recordDeployment, in both orders. The diff adds no race for it. Instead it adds a source-text guard that relies on an untested claim about createRelease, and the guard cannot reliably find callers. (1) It reads only server/services.ts. A call to assignProposals from sync/import.ts, chat.ts, mcp.ts or actions.ts is never seen. (2) It splits the file into segments that each start at `export const X = defineService(` and run to the next `\nexport const `. Any code in between belongs to the segment before it, such as an `export async function`, an `export default` or a non-exported helper. So a new caller defined after createRelease is counted as createRelease, and the sorted list stays the same. (3) It never checks that createRelease's release really is invisible. If two createRelease calls race for the same project and version, or createRelease races a recordDeployment that creates or looks up that version, nothing tests the result. Fix: add createRelease to the it.each race table with the holdAfterReleaseLock gate, in both orders. If you keep a guard, base it on imports and call sites across every module file, not on how services.ts happens to be laid out.

Instance fix of the round-17 finding. The finding asked for createRelease to be raced against a Prod recordDeployment in both orders. The diff adds one order only, and it races only against a deployment of the same new version. That deployment cannot find the release at all, so the 'no release v1' refusal holds with or without any locking. The race that can actually lose data crosses releases. createRelease(v2, [p]) holds a lock only on its own new v2 row, so nothing serialises it with a recordDeployment(Prod) of v1, which locks v1. The dangerous case is p already assigned to v1 while v1 goes to Prod. Neither order of that race is tested: createRelease held after the v2 insert while v1 deploys, and v1's deploy held after its release lock while createRelease(v2, [p]) runs. The same cross-release case is also missing for setReleaseProposals on a different release. Fix: add createRelease (and the cross-release setReleaseProposals case) to the it.each race table with holdAfterReleaseLock, in both orders. Assert that p ends up either released under v1 or unreleased under v2, never released with release_id = v2.

The round-17 fix is only partly a class fix. The `for update` lock is in the shared `assignProposals`, so the code covers both callers. The new cross-release race table only drives `createRelease(v2, [p])`, though. The previous finding also named the same cross-release race for `setReleaseProposals` on a different, already existing release, and that case still has no test in either order. `setReleaseProposals` locks its own release (v2) before calling `assignProposals`. Any read or check it makes before that call is not covered. If a later change moves its phase or release check ahead of the row lock, no test fails. Fix: add `setReleaseProposals(v2, [p])` rows to this `it.each` table, with v2 created empty beforehand. Cover move-first (hold on the `for update` select) and deploy-first (hold on the released update). Assert the same end states: proposed under v2, or released under v1 with 'already shipped in another release'.

The new row lock is taken one row at a time, in the caller's key order. A Prod deployment's `update delivery.proposal set phase = 'released' where release_id = …` locks the same rows in scan order, and two createRelease/setReleaseProposals calls lock them in whatever order their key lists give. With two or more shared proposals, the lock orders can cross. Postgres then aborts one transaction with a raw 40P01 'deadlock detected' error instead of a clear refusal or a serialised result. The new tests use a single proposal, so they cannot show this. Fix: lock every target row in one deterministic statement (`select … where key = any(${keys}) and project_id = … order by id for update`). Lock v1's proposal rows the same way (order by id) before the deploy's update. Then add a two-proposal race test.

In recordDeployment the new row lock comes after the `moved` read. The lock makes the deploy wait for a concurrent move, but the event list was already taken from the rows as they were before that move committed. Once the lock is granted, the update re-checks `release_id = v1` and skips the moved proposal. `moved` still includes it, so a ProposalPhaseChanged → released event is emitted for a proposal that was never released. The reverse also happens: a proposal assigned to v1 while the deploy waits is released by the update but gets no event. voidDeployment avoids this by taking its events from `update … returning *`. Fix: take the lock before the read and build the events from the update's `returning *`. Extend the move-first race rows to assert the outbox events, not just the row state.

The new deadlock test fires three writers with Promise.allSettled and hopes they interleave. A deadlock needs one writer to hold proposal a while another holds b, and nothing forces that. The other race tests in this file force their interleavings with holdAfterReleaseLock; this one does not. It is likely to stay green if lockProposals is reverted to the per-key `for update` loop, so it does not prove the round-19 fix. It also never checks the end state of a and b. Fix: make the race deterministic. Hold one writer after it has locked the first shared row (or after its ordered lock statement), start the opposite-order writer, release the hold, then assert both settle with no 40P01 and assert where a and b end up.

moveProposal reads the proposal without a row lock and then updates it unconditionally by id. Every other writer that changes a release's proposal rows locks them first (lockProposals, rounds 18 to 20). Because of that, a board/MCP/chat Move can overwrite the 'released' phase that a concurrent Prod deployment just set. The move's UPDATE waits on the deployment's lock, then re-checks only `id = ...` and goes ahead. Fix: read with `for update` (or use lockProposals) before the phase check, or make the update conditional (`where id = ... and phase <> 'released'`) and refuse when no row changed. Add a two-worker race test (move held vs. Prod deploy, both orders) that fails without the lock.

There are two rules for whether a release is live in Prod, and they disagree. nextStep/listReleases look at the latest non-voided record per environment (`status === 'deployed'` on Prod). assignProposals and voidDeployment look at any non-voided deployment with `released = true`. A later Prod record with status 'testing' or 'rolled-back' makes the map say the release isn't live, while the proposals stay Released and the service refuses new proposals as 'already live in Prod'. Use one definition, ideally the `released` flag, for both the map and the services.

Round 17 made a duplicate version in createRelease fail with a clear error, but two other duplicate-key paths still surface a raw Postgres unique violation: tagRelease renaming to a version the project already has, and createProject with an existing key. Use the same pattern on both (check, or `on conflict do nothing` and throw a clear error) and add variant tests.

releaseEditAction runs tagRelease and setReleaseProposals as two separate service transactions. If the second fails, the re-tag is already committed and the redirect never runs. The user stays on a page whose URL names a version that no longer exists, and the only error they see is about the proposals. Validate the proposals first, or do the re-tag and the proposal change in one service/transaction.

The contract read functions (listProjectRefs, getProjectRef, managedProjectIds) take only a tenant tx and apply no caller data scope or permission check. architecture.md says cross-module reads go through contract functions 'which apply the caller's data scope', and the file header claims they do. Take the caller's viewer/context and filter by delivery:read and its scope, or fix the header and doc claim.

The round-18/19 rule says every writer that changes a release's proposal rows locks them first. moveProposal breaks that rule. It reads the proposal with a plain select and then updates it by id with no lock and no phase guard. A board or MCP move that runs alongside a Prod recordDeployment is applied after the deploy commits and overwrites 'released'. Fix: lock the row the same way the other writers do (`lockProposals(tx, sql\`id = ${p.id}\`)`, or `select ... for update`) before reading the phase. Alternatively add `and phase = ${p.phase}` to the update and refuse when no row changes. Add a two-session race test against recordDeployment that uses holdAfterReleaseLock.

Lost wake-up race between block() and signalTx(). block() inserts the 'waiting' step, then looks for a buffered signal, all in one transaction. signalTx() inserts the signal and updates the waiting steps in another transaction. Under READ COMMITTED, neither transaction sees the other's uncommitted row. If both overlap, the signal is stored, no step is woken, and the run is set to waiting with wake_at = null. Nothing ever claims it again. Fix: serialise the two on (tenant, event), for example with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(tenant||event)) taken in both block() and signalTx() before the insert. Or re-check buffered signals after commit. Then add a two-session race test that fails without the fix.

The guarantees 'overlapping ticks never drive the same run' (claim_runs SKIP LOCKED plus lease fencing) and 'a retried tick never starts the same slot twice' (claim_schedules plus the slot key) have no test that runs two workers at the same time. kill.test.ts runs one worker after another has died, so it would still pass with SKIP LOCKED, the lease check or the fenced() guard removed. Add a test that runs two engine.tick() loops on separate connections against the same due runs and schedules, and asserts each step and each slot ran exactly once.

The lease is renewed only in loadRun, before a step runs. It is never renewed while the step runs. Any step whose run time is longer than leaseSeconds (300 s; step timeouts can be set to anything) is claimed again by the next tick and runs at the same time. The first worker's fenced() write then fails. Each later worker loses its lease the same way, so the step can never be recorded. Fix: heartbeat the lease while the step runs (and abort it when fencing is lost), or reject step timeouts at or above the lease.

The tick's time budget (budgetMs = 20 s) is checked only after a step has run inside driveRun. After the deadline, every claimed run that is left still gets loaded and runs one full step. One tick can therefore take batch × step timeout. Check the deadline before driving each claimed run, and release the leases of runs not driven (wake_at = now(), lease = null).

An exception from one schedule (validInput failing on the schedule's input, Temporal unreachable, a bad cron) leaves fireSchedules. That aborts the whole engine tick before claim_runs runs. The schedule is retried 60 s later and fails again, so no workflow run for any tenant is driven again. Catch per schedule: record the failure, for example as a failed run or last_status, release the lock, and continue. Then drive runs whatever happened in fireSchedules.

An entity schedule's zone comes from a fixed country map (LK, AU). Any other country falls back silently to UTC (coalesce(..., 'UTC') in ensure_schedules). The map also gives a single zone per country. A legal entity in an unmapped country, or in another AU zone, gets its '06:00' job at the wrong local time, and nothing flags it. Fail closed instead: refuse or flag schedules for entities without a known zone, and take the zone from the entity rather than a country map.

inputFor() adds legalEntityId to the input of entity schedules. engine.start() then runs validInput(), which passes the input through the workflow's zod schema. z.object() strips unknown keys by default, so legalEntityId is silently dropped whenever the workflow declares an input schema without it. Every entity's run then gets the same input. The test uses test.approval, which has no schema, so it does not catch this. Validate in workflowRegistry() that an entity schedule's workflow accepts legalEntityId, or pass the entity on ctx instead.

The retry policy is written twice and the two copies disagree. Postgres uses retryDelayMs, min(maxMs, initialMs*backoff^(n-1)). Temporal uses maximumInterval: max(maxMs, initialMs) and backoffCoefficient: max(1, backoff). The same definition therefore retries on a different schedule depending on the engine, which breaks AC-3 ('the same definitions'). Derive both from one function in duration.ts, for example by clamping in resolveStep.

Event matching is implemented twice. Postgres uses jsonb `payload @> wait_match` (signal.ts, drive.ts). Temporal uses a hand-written contains() in the workflow sandbox, and the two disagree on some inputs, so the same wait can match on one engine and not on the other. Make contains() follow jsonb containment exactly, and add a table test that runs both over the same cases.

start() calls launch() inside the caller's transaction, before it commits. StartOptions.tx promises that 'the run exists only if the caller's write commits'. For Temporal this does not hold: if the caller's transaction rolls back, the Temporal workflow still runs its steps, with external side effects, for a run row that does not exist. Even when the transaction commits, early mark() and runStep() calls can run before the row is visible. mark()'s UPDATE then matches 0 rows silently, so the mirror shows the wrong status. Launch after commit, for example through the outbox or a post-commit hook, or have mark() fail when it finds no row.

bridge.ts says outbox events wake a waiting run 'exactly once'. On Temporal, handle.signal() is an external call made inside the outbox delivery transaction. If that transaction rolls back after the signal was sent (a later handler fails, or the commit fails), the event is delivered again and the workflow's inbox holds two copies. The duplicate then satisfies a later wait with the same match. Deduplicate by event id: pass the outbox event id in the signal and ignore ids already seen in amaxRun.

The audit-chain check returns { ok: false, summary } when it finds tampering, so the run is recorded as 'completed'. The Runs list shows a 'good' chip, and the Failed runs ticket says 0 with 'None in the latest runs'. A failed integrity check reads as a pass, and nobody is notified. Throw NonRetryableError, or emit an event that notifications handles, when result.ok is false.

Setting workflows.engine: temporal only injects env vars into the web pod and into the worker pod, which only curls the tick endpoint (64Mi). Nothing in the chart or the app runs createTemporalWorker(), so Temporal has no worker polling the task queue. The temporal engine's tick() does not drive runs either. Every run started on Temporal stays queued. Add a Temporal worker Deployment, or entrypoint, that runs createTemporalWorker when the engine is temporal.

fireSchedules does not isolate failures per schedule. If start throws for one row (input fails the workflow's schema, the tenant's tx fails, Temporal is down), the error escapes the loop. The Postgres tick then never reaches claim_runs, so no run in any tenant is driven, and this repeats every minute. The other rows in that batch stay claimed for 60 s. Fix: wrap each row in try/catch, log it and count it as failed, release its lease, and keep going.

An attempt is only recorded after the step finishes (writeStep in recordStep). If the process dies mid-step (OOM, SIGKILL, or the host's function timeout on Vercel or Cloudflare while /api/jobs/tick runs a step whose timeout is longer than the request limit), no attempt is counted. The lease then expires and the step is re-claimed with the same attempt number, forever. maxAttempts never trips and the run never fails. The kill test even asserts attempts = 1 after a kill. The deadline is only checked between commands, so a single step can hold the request well past the budget. A step timeout longer than leaseSeconds (300 s) also lets a second worker claim and run the step while the first is still executing it. Fix: bump attempts in a committed write before executing the step, cap step timeout below the lease, and treat a crashed attempt as a failed one.

temporal() memoises the Connection.connect promise with ??=. If the first connect fails (frontend restarting, DNS blip), the rejected promise is cached and every later start, signal and control call in that process fails until restart. workflowEngine() in apps/web/lib/server.ts caches its promise the same way. Fix: clear the cached promise on rejection.

The two engines disagree on events that arrive before a run reaches its wait. Postgres buffers every signal created since the run started (takeBufferedSignal), whatever waitsFor says. Temporal only sends the signal to runs whose workflow lists the event in waitsFor, or that are already waiting, so for other workflows an early event is dropped. AC-3 promises the same behaviour on both engines, and the conformance suite only covers a workflow that declares waitsFor. Fix: buffer the same way on both engines (for example, always deliver to active runs of workflows that call waitForEvent for that event, or have Postgres also require waitsFor), and add the case to the suite.

workflows.run records which workflow ran but not which version of its definition, and replay matches history by step name only. A deploy that renames, reorders or inserts steps while runs are sleeping or waiting resumes them on the new code against old history. Renamed steps run again, which duplicates side effects, and their old checkpoints are silently ignored. Fix: store a definition version or hash on the run, and refuse or route resumes on a mismatch (Temporal-style patching).

The claims that 'SKIP LOCKED plus the lease mean overlapping ticks never drive the same run' (claim_runs plus the fencing token) and 'a retried tick never starts the same slot twice' (claim_schedules) have no test with two concurrent workers. The kill test is sequential: the child is killed before the parent ticks. Both tests would stay green with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or the lease check removed. Add a test that runs two engine.tick() loops on separate connections against the same due runs and schedules, and asserts each step executes once and each slot fires once.

controlRun and setScheduleEnabled hand-roll the write pipeline. They authorise with a role-string check (assertAdmin) instead of the service pipeline and can(), and they write and audit directly, so no event is emitted. architecture.md requires every write to go authorize → validate → write → audit → emit. This is a second copy of the authorise/audit logic that can drift from defineService: grants, data scopes and View as handling are not applied, and nothing downstream can react to a cancelled run or a disabled schedule. Fix: route both through defineService with workflows permissions and emitted events.

Retention periods are written twice. workflowsRetention declares P1Y/P30D, and pruneRunsJob hard-codes interval '1 year' and '30 days', so changing one leaves the other stale. The workflows.step entry also starts at step finished_at. When 032's enforcer applies it, it will delete the done checkpoints of runs that are still active (waiting or sleeping for over a year). On resume those steps run again. Fix: derive the job's SQL from the entries, and key step retention on the parent run's finished_at.

ensure_schedules falls back to UTC for any entity country missing from ENTITY_ZONES (coalesce(..., 'UTC')), and ENTITY_ZONES only knows LK and AU. A schedule declared to run in each entity's zone then silently runs at the wrong local time. Fix: fail closed. Flag or skip the schedule and surface the missing zone instead of defaulting.

Some writes skip the service pipeline that architecture.md requires for every write (authorize → validate → write → audit → emit). revokeLapsedVersions revokes credential versions and destroys their ciphertext with no audit record. warnExpiring writes to core.event by hand with raw SQL, which is a second copy of the outbox emit. useSecret (use.ts:36) updates secrets.credential.last_used_* outside defineService. Fix: run the sweep's revocations and warnings through a defineService job service, so each revocation is audited and each event goes out through the pipeline's emit. Do the same for the last-used update, or record it as part of the audited use.

dataKeyFor() puts a newly created data key into the process cache before the transaction that inserts its secrets.data_key row has committed. If that transaction rolls back (in putSecret, any later failure: the version insert, the audit write, event emit or idempotency settle), the cache still holds a key that no row records. For up to 5 minutes, the next putSecret calls on that instance hit the cache, seal values with that key and commit. Once the cache expires or the process restarts, dataKeyFor finds no row and wraps a new key. The committed ciphertexts can then never be opened: the credentials are lost. Fix: cache a key only after its row is known to be committed. Either create the data key in its own committed transaction, then re-read and cache it, or cache only on the path that read an existing row. Add a test where a putSecret fails after dataKeyFor, then a second putSecret succeeds, then the cache is cleared, then useSecret runs.

The check that keeps values inside useSecret only catches the named case: the raw value, its base64 and its encodeURIComponent form, found in JSON.stringify output. It misses several variants. (1) The callback can return the Secret itself, or an object holding it: toJSON prints "[secret]", so the check passes and the caller can call reveal() later, outside useSecret, with no audit. (2) A Map, Set or class instance holding the value serialises to {} and passes. (3) Encoded forms that are not checked pass: hex, base64url, base64 of `user:${value}` (Basic auth), JSON-escaped values, and form-encoding with '+'. (4) scrubError does not scrub error.name. Fix: reject any result that contains a Secret instance, walk Maps, Sets and objects instead of relying on JSON.stringify, and widen the forms checked to hex, base64url and JSON-escaped.

useSecret and useValidSecrets decrypt a tenant credential for any ServiceContext and never call authorize(). putSecret, revokeSecret and listCredentials are all permission-checked, but the read of the plaintext is not. Any module code path running under a non-admin user's ui, mcp or chat context can decrypt any connector's credential, including msgraph-write ('Approved access changes only'). Fix: authorize a secrets:credential:use permission, scoped per connector and per caller kind, before load(), and throw ForbiddenError when it is refused.

formsOf() only covers three encodings of the value: raw, standard base64 and encodeURIComponent. assertNoLeak and scrubError both rely on it, so any other encoding passes as clean. Missed variants: base64 of `id:secret`, which is how HTTP Basic auth sends client credentials (common for Xero and other OAuth token endpoints); base64url; hex; and JSON-escaped values. serialised() runs JSON.stringify, so a value that contains `"` or `\\` appears escaped and no longer matches. Fix: also check base64url, hex, the JSON-escaped form and the URLSearchParams form. For Basic auth, either give connectors a helper that registers the derived header value as a form, or check substrings of decoded base64 runs. Extend the AC-2 test to a table over these variants.

The year-ago window end is built by string surgery (`${year-1}${today.slice(4)}`) and then cast with `::date`. On 29 February that makes an impossible date (e.g. 2027-02-29), so Postgres throws and pipelineStats fails. That breaks both the board page and the pipeline_summary MCP tool. Compute it with date arithmetic instead (`${today}::date - interval '1 year'`, or setUTCFullYear), and add tests for 2028-02-29, 2028-03-01 and an ordinary day.

`change` is null when either window has no closed deals, and every null gets the same note: "No deals closed the year before". If the current 12 months have no closed deals but the year before does, the ticket shows '–' with a false reason. Branch on which side is null.

insertOpportunity says the advisory lock serialises concurrent creates so numbers stay gapless and unique. No test runs two real sessions creating at once. Deleting the lock leaves every test green: two concurrent creates then both read the same max(number), and one fails on unique(tenant_id, number) instead of getting the next number. Add a two-session race test (createOpportunity × 2 and acceptSuggestion + createOpportunity) that fails without the lock.

promoteToDelivery checks 'not yet promoted' in a read transaction, calls delivery's create, and only then locks the opportunity in recordPromotion. Two concurrent promotes of the same won opportunity with different keys both pass the check and both create a delivery project. recordPromotion then rejects the second with 'already project X', leaving an orphaned delivery project. Serialise on the opportunity before creating (for example, claim it under lock first), or have the loser find and void its project. Add a two-session race test.

'Open in chat' sends the inbox agent's summary, text taken from external email and Teams, into the chat as the user's own prompt (`${s.client}: ${s.summary}`). The module standard requires untrusted text to be passed as data. Pass the suggestion id or a quoted data field to the intent, not free-text prompt content.

recordPromotion stops two opportunities from sharing a project with a check-then-write: a `select ... where project_id = $1 and id <> $2` followed by an update. The only lock is on the opportunity's own row, and the schema has no unique constraint on project_id. Two different opportunities promoted at the same time take different row locks, so both pass the check. promoteToDelivery's retry path makes this reachable: it adopts an existing project whose name and client match. Add `unique (tenant_id, project_id)` (partial, where project_id is not null) to opportunity, or lock on the project id.

The fix dropped the old check that an adopted project's name and client match the opportunity. Now a resumed claim links whatever delivery project has that key. claimPromotion sets `resumed = true` whenever a stale claim has the same key, but it does not check that the claim actually created that project. promoteToDelivery then links `existing` without checking it either. Fix: record the project id on the claim once delivery creates it, and resume only that project. At minimum, put back the name and client match before adopting.

The 120 s claim is a lease that nothing checks against. A claim under another key is replaced if delivery has no project with that key yet, but the old attempt may still be creating it. Nothing stops that attempt's create from finishing later. Its recordPromotion then fails the token check and leaves an orphaned project. That is the same orphan the round-1 finding named, now reached through the timeout. Fix: re-check the claim token in the same transaction as the create (or right before it), or let the loser void its project. Add a race test with a create stub slower than CLAIM_SECONDS.

The round-1 finding about two opportunities sharing one project was fixed with the partial unique index `opportunity_project`, but no test covers it. review.test.ts only races one opportunity against itself. Add a table-driven test that links the same project id from two opportunities, both one after the other and concurrently, and through the resumed-claim path. Each must fail without the index.

The untrusted text is gone, but so is any reference to the suggestion. Every 'Open in chat' button now sends the same fixed prompt, so chat cannot tell which find the user opened. The finding asked for the suggestion id, or a quoted data field, to be passed to the intent. Pass `s.id` as structured intent data, and have the chat intent load the suggestion itself as data.

setTaskStatus and setRiskStatus now use lockOpenOpportunity, so tasks and risks on a won or lost deal can never be closed. No round-1 finding asked for this. Blocking new records on closed deals may be intended, but status changes on existing ones should stay allowed (or the open ones should be closed automatically when the deal closes).

The promotion tests cover only two variants: the concurrent race with different keys, and a failed create with a retry. Three paths have no test. (1) The resume path that the docstring promises: the project was created, the link failed, and a retry with the same key links that project and makes no second one. (2) The stale-claim takeover with a different key, both with and without the claimed project in delivery. (3) The new unique index `opportunity_project`, which is the fix for the previous round's shared-project finding: no test promotes two opportunities onto the same project and expects the second to be refused. Add table rows that drive each case through promoteToDelivery or the services. Make each one fail when its guard is removed.

newPeriod only rewrites the one period in force on `effectiveOn`. Periods that already start later keep the old department, grade, manager, contract and salary, so the change is quietly undone when the next period starts. The fixtures plant these later periods for the 6 part-timers who go full time (FULL_TIME_FROM).
