Fix: also apply `set` to every hr.employment row with `starts_on > on` for this person, or reject the change when later periods exist. Add a variant test for: no later period, one later FTE step, and two later steps.

recordLeaver ends only the periods with `starts_on <= leftOn`. A period that starts after the leave date keeps `ends_on = null`, so the leaver still looks employed in that period with no end. This hits a future FTE step and also a 'joining' person who leaves before their start date. Fix: delete those later periods, or end them too, and test both variants.

Person status is decided once, at write time. The module has `jobs: []`, so nothing ever moves a person from 'joining' to 'active' once joinedOn passes, or to 'left' once a future leftOn passes. Headcount, the directory chips, 'upcoming', reportUserIds and listPeople({status}) all go stale. The module standard says waiting work must be a @amax/workflows schedule. Fix: add a daily job that applies the transitions through a service, or derive status from the dates when reading.

Person-level fields (title, location, workEmail) are written to hr.person straight away, whatever `effectiveOn` says. Yet the hr.person.changed event and the audit `after` both record them as effective on that date. Fix: reject effectiveOn for person-only fields, or schedule them, and make the event reflect what actually took effect.

entityOf resolves free text with `name ilike %entity%` and `order by name limit 1`. Input that matches several legal entities, or that contains a `%`/`_` wildcard, silently picks the alphabetically first one. The person is then created in that entity's employee series and currency. Fix: match exactly on id, country or name, and fail when there are zero matches or more than one.

getEmployment gives unmasked pay and bank data (salary, EPF, bank account) to any caller that passes the string "system". Nothing authenticates that claim and nothing audits the read. architecture.md says contract reads 'apply the caller's data scope', but any module or chat/MCP code path can call it with "system". listPeople, getPerson and listEmploymentPeriods also take no viewer at all. Fix: take a ServiceContext or a real system actor that core issues, check it, and audit unmasked reads.

nextEmployeeNo claims numbering is 'serialised per tenant' through pg_advisory_xact_lock, but no test runs two addPerson calls at once. A single-session test stays green if the lock is deleted. Add a race test with two real sessions that asserts two distinct, consecutive numbers.

inScope skips the legal-entity scope check whenever viewerOf(ctx) returns nothing. Any context without a viewer (an agent, a workflow, or a contract command) therefore gets unscoped HR writes. Fail closed: when there is no viewer, check the actor's scope another way or reject.

An unknown `/hr/e/:entity` code falls back to entity=undefined and renders the whole company under that URL. Commit 0853a72 fixed only the client-side select, not the server route. Legal entities are also keyed by country code, so two entities in the same country share a code and the second is unreachable. Fix: return notFound() for an unknown code, and give each entity a unique key.

'Employment in force' is written three times, and the copies use different clocks. CURRENT (contracts.ts:44) uses the DB's `current_date`. peopleStats' departments lateral uses the JS `today` passed in. getEmployment uses `new Date().toISOString()` (UTC). The directory, the department chart and the employment card can therefore disagree around midnight and in tests. Fix: use one parameterised SQL fragment that takes the as-of date, everywhere.

`employment.ends_on` stands for two things: the end of an effective-dated period (set by newPeriod and the FTE steps) and the end of the contract. contractsEndingNextMonth counts any fixed-term period boundary as a contract ending. EmploymentCard shows the period end as 'ends <date>' even on permanent contracts. Fix: store the contract end in its own column (or on the person), or count and show only the last period's ends_on.

getEmployment returns unmasked pay, EPF and bank details to any caller that passes the string literal "system". This is a public contract, so any module (including its MCP or chat tools acting for a user) can bypass 002 masking by typing one string. Fix: require an unforgeable system capability (for example a token from @amax/core that only workflows and the runtime can mint), or expose a separate, audited system read.

The new update copies every changed column into all later periods without checking whether a later period already sets that column itself. If the changed column is the one a planned step changes (fte, base_salary, next_review, contract, grade), the plan is silently overwritten. The fix only handles the reported case, where an unrelated column (department) carries forward. The variant test covers only a department change, never a change to fte or salary. Fix: copy a column into a later period only where that period's value still equals the old in-force value (cur[col]). Otherwise reject the change or ask the caller to choose. Extend the table test with an fte change ahead of an fte step and a salary change ahead of a planned raise.

The previous blocker named four contract reads. This diff fixed only one (getEmployment). getPerson, listPeople and listEmploymentPeriods still take no viewer and apply no data scope or hr:read check. architecture.md requires cross-module reads to 'apply the caller's data scope'. The new header comment calls them safe because they return no classified field, but that does not scope them. Any module can list every person in every legal entity, including leavers with their leave dates, for a user who has no hr:read or is scoped to one entity. Fix: take the caller's Viewer (or ServiceContext) in every contract read and filter by legal-entity scope, as getEmployment now does.

With the 'system' reader removed, the contract offers no way for trusted, viewer-less code to read pay. The comment and README tell payroll to 'add its own audited system read'. Under the module standard, payroll may not read hr.employment directly (imports limited to other modules' contracts.ts; reads go through contract functions). So the documented path either breaks the boundary law or leaves payroll with no data. Fix: give the contract an explicit, audited system read that requires an actor core issues (for example a job/system ServiceContext checked like inScope), and document that instead.

The SQL fragment is now shared, but the as-of date is still not, so the earlier clock finding was only partly fixed. peopleStats takes a JS Date and derives `now` itself. listDirectory, getPerson, listPeople, reportUserIds and getPersonView call today() inside, with no parameter. PeoplePage passes its own `new Date()` to peopleStats while the directory calls today() separately, and tests can pin the date for stats but not for the directory. Fix: pass one as-of date through every read (directory, contract reads, stats), defaulting once at the entry point.

recordLeaver now hard-deletes later employment periods (planned FTE steps, raises, or a joiner's whole employment). The audit records only `before: { status }`, so the deleted rows (salary, grade, FTE, dates) are not in any audit record and cannot be restored if the leaver was recorded by mistake. The module standard requires every write to be audited. Fix: put the deleted periods in the audit `before`, or end and void them instead of deleting.

The carry-forward check compares every later period with the value in force at `effectiveOn` (`cur[col]`). It should compare with the value of the period just before it. A later period that plans a return to the old value (an FTE step down and then back up, or a temporary acting grade that then reverts) holds a value equal to `cur[col]`, so it is overwritten as if it had only inherited that value. The new table test has just one later period, so it can't catch this. Fix: walk the later periods in `starts_on` order and stop carrying a column at the first period whose value differs from the period before it, or compare each period with its predecessor. Add a test with a step down followed by a step back up.

This is the same class as the earlier 'system' string blocker. The new code decides who gets unmasked pay and bank data from a structural field (`actor.kind === "system"`) on a plain object, and any caller can forge that object. The diff's own test builds a ServiceContext literal by hand (`{ tenantId, actor: { id, kind }, source } as ServiceContext`). Set `kind: "system"` instead and any module, chat or MCP path gets salary, EPF and bank account for every entity. The audit row then records the forged actor id. The previous finding asked for an actor that core issues and checks. Fix: accept only contexts made by `contextFor.job` (for example, a core-private brand or WeakSet checked through a core verifier), and add a test showing that a hand-built system context is refused.

recordLeaver's audit still can't undo a mistaken leaver, so this fixes only the case that was named. First, the removed periods leave out base_salary (only `hadPay` is kept), along with currency, epf_number, bank_name, bank_account and the row ids, so a deleted planned raise can't be restored. Second, the next statement overwrites `ends_on` on the period in force, and the old end date is not in `before` at all. Fix: end and void the later periods instead of deleting them, so the data stays in the table, or keep the full rows somewhere they can be restored from. Also record the old `ends_on` of every period the update changes.

`sees` passes only `{ legalEntityId }` to `can(viewer, 'hr:read', ...)`. But role assignments also carry `departments` (the tests set `departments: null`). An HR assignment limited to some departments is either granted the whole entity or decided without the row's department. The row already has the department (`emp.department` in people(), `department` in the employment rows). Fix: pass the row's department, along with every other scope dimension the auth model has, to the same subject used for masking. Add a department-scoped case to the scoping table test.

After this fix, employment periods are read through the viewer's hr data scope (`listEmploymentPeriods(tx, v, ids)`), but team membership and allocation totals are still read without that scope. When a team member falls outside the viewer's hr scope, hr returns no period for them. `fteIn` then returns 0, so the person is treated as 'not employed'. They drop out of capacity, demand and bench with no sign that anything was hidden, so 'could not see' reads the same as 'nothing there'. The grid has the same root cause: `gridIn` (grid.ts:25) filters people through `listPeople(tx, v, { ids })` while `peopleIn` keeps every allocation, so hidden people vanish and the screen shows 'No allocations yet'. Fix: decide what a narrow-scope viewer should see. Either compute the team aggregates (capacity, demand, bench) from an unscoped, system read and mask only the person-level fields, or return an explicit `hidden: n` / 'partial' flag that the screen and MCP show. Add a variant test with at least three viewers (Leadership, PM, an HR viewer limited to Australia) so that dropping or keeping the scoping changes the result. The current tests only use maya as Leadership or PM, and they pass with or without the scoping.

`mayAllocate` returns true whenever `viewerOf(ctx)` is missing (`!v || can(...)`). A ServiceContext without a viewer, such as a job, agent or contract-command context, skips the project-scope check entirely. `copyMonth` inherits this through its `allowed` filter. When the viewer is missing, this should deny or require an explicit system actor that is checked by kind, not grant unscoped allocation.

When `through` is earlier than `month`, `monthsBetween` returns only `[from]`. The reversed range is accepted without error and only one month is written. The range is also unbounded. Fix: add a `.refine` that `through >= month` and cap the span, for example at 24 months.

This round makes allocations read the hr contract with the caller's data scope ('scoped hr v2 contract'). Its own published contract reads, `listAllocations` and `personMonthTotals`, still take no caller context and return every person's allocations in the tenant. architecture.md says cross-module reads go through contract functions 'which apply the caller's data scope', and the same class was already fixed in hr. Fix: give the contract reads a ServiceContext/Viewer parameter, filter by the caller's scope (for example managed/assigned projects or the people the caller may see), and version the contract (v2) with a README note.

This is an instance fix, and it repeats the class that was already reported as a blocker in hr/contracts.ts. When there is no viewer, `mayAllocate` now trusts `ctx.actor.kind === "system"`. That is a structural field on a plain object, and any code path that builds a ServiceContext literal can set it. The diff's own test builds such a literal by hand (`{ tenantId: T, actor: { id: "sp:x", kind: "service" }, ... } as never`). Changing `"service"` to `"system"` turns that same literal into an unscoped writer. This is also a second copy of the 'is this a trusted system context' rule (B4): hr decides trust for `contextFor.job` contexts itself, and the two checks can disagree. Fix: use the single unforgeable system-context check that core/hr uses for `contextFor.job` (a brand or registry check, not a field check). Add a variant that proves a hand-built `{ actor: { kind: "system" } }` literal is refused.

This is a class miss of last round's B3 finding. The grid now reports `hidden`, but the newly scoped contract reads do not. `visible()` silently drops the rows of people the reader can't see, so `listAllocations` and `personMonthTotals` return `[]` both for 'this person has no allocations' and for 'you may not see this person'. A consuming module can't tell these apart and will read a hidden person as 0% allocated, or as on the bench. Fix: return the hidden person ids or a count with the result (for example `{ rows, hidden }`), or throw or flag when requested `personIds` fall outside the scope. Cover this with a variant test over Leadership, AU-limited HR, and an explicit out-of-scope `personIds` request.

This is an instance fix of last round's B3 finding. `hidden` only counts people who have allocation rows in the range (`ids` comes from `rows`). A requested `personIds` entry that is out of scope and has no rows gives `{ rows: [], hidden: 0 }`. That is the same answer as "you may see this person and they have nothing allocated", so the read still reports "could not ask" as "nothing there". Counting this way also leaks something: an out-of-scope reader can query one id at a time and learn whether a person they may not see has any allocations (hidden 1 vs 0). Fix: when `personIds` is given, check those ids against `listPeople(tx, reader, { ids: personIds })` and count every requested id outside the scope, whether or not it has rows. When `personIds` is not given, keep the current count. Add a variant where the AU-limited reader asks for an out-of-scope person who has no rows in the month and expect `hidden: 1`.

The new copyMonth test accepts two outcomes for a context with no viewer that isn't a system context: an error, or `{ copied: 0, skipped: N>0 }`. The second outcome is what copyMonth actually returns: its `allowed` filter drops the rows it is not allowed to copy and counts them as `skipped`. That is the same `skipped` count used for 'already present in the next month'. So 'you are not allowed to copy' looks like 'nothing left to copy', and the test locks that ambiguity in. Fix: make copyMonth throw forbidden (as allocate does) when the context has no viewer and isSystemContext(ctx) is false. Or return forbidden/hidden separately from skipped. Then tighten the test to expect only that outcome.

Instance fix. The WeakSet stops hand-built literals, but the factory that mints trust is still public. `contextFor` is exported from `@amax/core/server`, and every module, chat intent and MCP tool may import that package; `modules/hr/server/jobs.ts` already calls `contextFor.job` from module code. Any caller can therefore run `contextFor.job(anyTenantId, "anything")` and get a context that `isSystemContext` accepts. That context reads unmasked salary, EPF and bank data through getEmployment and passes inScope and applyStatusDates. The audit row records a job name the caller made up. The issued object is also not frozen. Only `actor.kind` is checked again, so `ctx.actor.id`, `tenantId` and `onBehalfOf` can be changed after issue and the context still passes. Fix: only the job runner (runDueJobs or the workflow engine) should be able to mint system contexts, through an unexported capability or a factory that is not on the module import surface. The runner then hands the context to the job handler. Freeze the issued context and its actor. Add a test showing that module-level code can't get an accepted system context.

This only fixes one case of the earlier blocker. Freezing the context stops callers changing it after issue. The main part of the finding is not fixed: `contextFor.job` is still exported from `@amax/core/server`, and every module, chat intent and MCP tool can import it. Any code can still call `contextFor.job(anyTenantId, "made-up")` and get a context that `isSystemContext` accepts. That context reads unmasked pay and bank data through getEmployment and passes `inScope` and `applyStatusDates`. The audit row then records a job name the caller invented. `modules/hr/server/jobs.ts:11` still mints its own context, and the diff adds no test showing that module code can't get an accepted system context. Fix: only the job runner (runDueJobs or the workflow engine) should mint system contexts, through a capability or factory that is not on the module import surface. The runner passes the context to the handler. Add a test showing that importing `@amax/core/server` from module code does not yield an accepted system context.

The department scope for writes is taken from the employment in force today (`employmentAt(today())`). The write itself is applied at `effectiveOn`, and `newPeriod` also rewrites later periods. So the check looks at a different period from the one being changed. A department change is also not checked against the department it moves the person into. Fix: check scope against the department of every period the write touches (the period in force on `effectiveOn` and every later period it rewrites). When the input sets `department`, check the target department too.

This fixes only the case that was named, not the whole class. copyMonth now throws when there is no viewer. But when a viewer is present, the `allowed` filter still drops rows outside the viewer's project scope and counts them in `skipped`. That is the same counter used for 'already present in the next month'. So 'you may not copy these' still looks like 'nothing left to copy' to any real user whose scope covers only part of the team. The last round asked for either a refusal or a separate count, and this applies it to the no-viewer path only. Fix: return forbidden rows as their own count (for example `hidden` or `forbidden`), separate from `skipped`. Add a test row with a viewer who has partial scope and expect that count to be greater than 0 and `skipped` to count only the rows already present.

The CSV export quotes each cell but does not neutralise formula prefixes. Proposal titles, owner names and project names come from untrusted paths (chat, MCP, specclaw sync), so a cell that starts with =, +, - or @ runs as a formula when the file is opened in Excel or Sheets. Fix: prefix any cell starting with = + - @, tab or CR with a single quote before escaping.

The new `!r.stages.some((s) => s.status) ? "Building"` branch runs before the `allowed` check. Users who may record deployments therefore lose the first-deploy button for any release that has no deployment yet. Before this change, only users without the permission saw "Building". Fix: put that branch inside the `!allowed` case, as before.

weekly_stat stores the portfolio total as the project_id-null row, and per-project rows sit in the same table (the migration says 008 will write both). weeklyThroughput and shippedPerWeek still `sum()` every row for the week with no project_id filter, so the portfolio is counted twice. Fix: filter `project_id is null` for the portfolio, or drop the null row and sum only the per-project rows.

"Shipped to Prod" is now counted in two places that can disagree. shippedPerWeek reads a hand-seeded roll-up that nothing in the app writes. phaseCounts' 'Released this month', on the same page, comes from proposal.released_at. Fix: derive shipped-per-week from released_at/deployments, or have the promote path write the roll-up inside the same service.

A week with no weekly_stat row is shown as 0 planned, 0 done and 0 shipped. No ingestion (008) exists yet, so every real tenant gets charts of zeros, plus a trend computed from those zeros, that look like real data. Fix: return null for missing weeks and render an empty state ('no data yet') instead of 0.

`today()` reads `process.env.AMAX_TODAY` directly in module code. The module standard says environment access goes through `@amax/core` adapters, and the architecture says config is validated at boot. As a result the value is never validated, and it applies to the whole process rather than per tenant, although the comment says it pins 'the demo tenant'. Fix: read it through the core config adapter, validate it as a date at boot, and scope it if per-tenant pinning is what's intended.

Pluralisation and client counts are mixed up. The lede uses the filtered client count but pluralises on `clients.length` (all clients). The ticket note always says 'clients'. Fix: compute the filtered client count once and pluralise on that same number in both places.

A proposal's release now comes from two places: the `release_id` join, or `meta.releaseLabel` if that is missing. The fixture moves CON-009 onto that label and deletes the CON v2.3.0 release and its Prod deployment. The result is a released proposal with no release, and production query code that reads a fixture-only field. Fix: keep CON-009 linked to a real v2.3.0 release (the map can hide old releases with its 45-day filter) and drop the meta fallback.

'Last reached stage' and 'is live' are now worked out in three places. `mapPill` sorts by position and treats the release as live only when that last stage is Prod. `mapRow`'s `last`/`lineTo` positions the pill. The map's 45-day filter has its own inline 'Prod deployed' check, and the table uses `nextStep`. With per-project environments (042) these can disagree. Fix: derive the last stage and liveness once, in `mapRow`/`nextStep`, and use that everywhere.

Change 041 is a delivery-module change, but this round edits platform code: packages/core/src/env.ts (AMAX_TODAY, clockFromEnv), packages/core/src/service.ts (Runtime.now, now()), packages/core/src/server.ts (the export) and apps/web/lib/server.ts (the wiring). The module standard says a module change touches only modules/<name>/ plus one CODEOWNERS line, and the architecture says the platform team owns packages/ and apps/web. Fix: move the core clock adapter and its web wiring into its own platform-lane change, and have 041 depend on it. 041 then only calls now() from @amax/core/server.

onActiveMap decides 'superseded' by the release row's createdAt (when the row was inserted), not by which release is newer in deployment order. A release recorded later can therefore hide the one that is actually current: a backfilled older version, or one imported by specclaw sync. Fix: treat a Live release as superseded only by a same-project release whose first deployment is later than this release's Prod deployment (or compare by version order). Add a test case where the older release has the later createdAt.

The 'missing week is null' fix only handles the case where every week is missing. In that case ProjectsPage shows its empty state. When only some weeks are missing, LineChart drops the null points and then runs `curve(pts)` and the area fill straight across the gap. The chart then shows a smooth line and shaded area through a week that has no roll-up, so it looks like real data. Only the screen-reader table says 'No data'. Fix: break the path into one segment per run of consecutive non-null points, and do the same for the area. Never interpolate across a null. Add a variant test with a null in the middle, a null at the start and a null at the end.

Only part of the supersession fix is a class fix. firstAt is described as 'first deployed', but it reads each environment's latest non-voided deployment. listReleases picks those with `distinct on (release_id, environment_id) ... order by at desc`. firstAt also counts a stage with any status, failed included, as a deployment. So a release that was redeployed or retried, or that only failed, can hide the release that is actually Live. The rule for 'has reached a stage' now also exists twice: firstAt has its own test (`s.status && s.at`) next to standing(), which the old code used through `standing(o).last`. The two can disagree (B4). Fix: decide supersession from the other release's earliest successful deployment. Either have listReleases return a first_deployed_at (min(at) where status = 'deployed' and not voided), or build it from standing(). Then add table rows for a failed-only newer release and for a retried Dev deployment.

The comment '0009 may already be applied' only covers databases that applied the original 0009 (the one with `shipped`). Round 1 (fd15dfe) edited 0009 to remove `shipped`, and this round edits 0009 again to put it back. A database migrated at round 1 has weekly_stat without `shipped`, so 0010's unconditional `drop column shipped` fails and the migration chain stops there. Also, if the runner checksums applied files, 0009 has changed under it twice. Fix: don't edit 0009 again; make 0010 `drop column if exists shipped`.

The supersession fix still covers only one ordering: the other release's first deployment comes after this one's Prod. When two releases overlap, the newer one can be deployed to an early stage before the older one reaches Prod. Its firstAt is then earlier than the older one's prodAt, so the older Live release is never marked superseded, even after the newer one reaches Prod. Fix: also treat a Live release as superseded when another release of the same project reached Prod later (compare live.at values), or when another release's latest deployment comes after this Prod deployment. Add rows for overlapping releases to the Active-map table.

The round-3 redesign counts a release as 'in flight' when it has reached a stage and is not Live (`!x.s.live`). That test cannot tell a release that is moving from one that was abandoned or rolled back. Any such release is kept with no age limit (the 45-day window applies only to Live ones). It also suppresses the project's current Live release completely. A Dev deployment that stalled or failed long ago therefore keeps the real Live release off the map forever. Before this round, that release was still shown. The 'only failed' row encodes this: a failed-only v2 hides the Live v1. Fix: treat a release as in flight only when its latest reached stage is newer than the project's current Live Prod deployment, or apply the same 45-day window to it. Ignore voided, rolled-back or failed-only releases older than the current Live one. Add table rows for (a) an old abandoned Dev-only release next to a recent Live one, and (b) an older release whose Prod deploy was rolled back next to a newer Live one.

The 'Tasks done per week' chart has its y-axis fixed at `max={40}`. Any week with more than 40 planned or done tasks is drawn above the plot area (`.chart{overflow:visible}`) against the 40 gridline, so the chart misreports the value. ProposalsPage already sizes its bar chart from the data, so the two charts behave differently. Fix: derive max from the series, e.g. `Math.max(40, ceil(max(planned, done) / step) * step)`.

The clock pin moved 'today' for the windows but did not bound them at today. phaseCounts counts released_at >= the 1st of the pinned month with no upper bound, and shippedPerWeek has no upper bound either. As soon as a tenant's pin is earlier than real time, releases after the pin are counted. weeklyThroughput is not affected because it matches weeks exactly. Fix: add `released_at < <start of next month>` to phaseCounts (and `< next Monday` to shippedPerWeek), and add a test with a pin earlier than a recorded release.

Other modules call `weekTotals` and `projectHours`, but these functions take only a `tx` and return every person's hours, status and name in the tenant. No caller viewer is passed and no data scope is applied. architecture.md says that 'Cross-module reads go through contract functions, which apply the caller's data scope'. Fix: take the caller's Viewer or ServiceContext, then filter rows the same way `seesWeek`/`time:team` does. Alternatively, publish only aggregates with no per-person data.

Week totals are worked out two ways that can disagree. TeamRow.total (and so the lede, the This week card and the 'Approve N submitted (X h)' button) adds up only the five Mon–Fri `perDay` cells. myWeek.total, weekHours (the submit payload) and the weekTotals contract add up every entry in the week. logTime takes any YYYY-MM-DD, including Saturday and Sunday, and its default 'today' can be a weekend. Fix: either reject weekend days in logTime, or show 7 days and compute every total from all the entries.

When no day is given, the default is `isoDate(new Date())`, which is the UTC date and not the person's local date. For tenants east or west of UTC, time logged near midnight lands on the wrong day, and on a Monday or Sunday it can land in a different ISO week. `today()` in ui/parts.tsx has the same UTC assumption. Fix: resolve 'today' in the tenant's or user's time zone, or require the caller to give a day.

guardLock blocks writes only when the week is 'approved'. Entries can still be added to a 'submitted' week. The approver then approves hours the person never submitted, and the WeekSubmitted.hours payload no longer matches. Fix: refuse logTime on submitted weeks, or move the week back to draft and require it to be submitted again.

The README rule 'you never approve your own week' is applied in chainFor, but the locked-change path lets any time:admin holder add hours to their own approved week. Those hours then sit in an approved, locked week that nobody else approved. Fix: in guardLock, reject a locked change when week.user_id is the actor's own user.

findWeek matches `person` by email OR by a case-insensitive person_name, then takes the first row. When two people share a name, approve_week, reject_week, remind_week and reopen_week act on whichever row comes first. Fix: fetch all matches and throw when there is more than one ('which Nimal Silva? use their email').

`wk()` turns a well-formed but non-existent ISO week into `undefined`, so get_team_week and get_my_week quietly fall back to the latest week. TeamPage and MyPage do the same with `parseWeekKey(params.week) ?? undefined`. Malformed input should produce an error (weekOrNow in server/weeks.ts already throws for this), not a different week's data.

logTime only checks whether the week is 'approved'. Anyone can still add entries to a week that is 'submitted', and the week stays submitted. The approver then approves and locks hours that were not there when the week was submitted. The WeekSubmitted payload also keeps the old total. Fix: when someone logs into a submitted week, either reject the write or move the week back to draft (with audit and an event). Add a test that logs into a submitted week.

The two contract reads apply the data scope differently. weekTotals calls `seesWeek` with all of the week's project ids, so a project manager who can see a week gets every hour in it, including hours on other projects. projectHours calls `seesWeek` with only `[projectId]` for each row, so the same viewer sees only their own project. The README says both functions return 'weeks they could see on Team time'. As written they give different totals for the same viewer and the same week. Fix: write one scope rule, either week-level or entry-level, and use it in both. Add a test where a PM's report has hours on a project the PM doesn't manage.

The test for 'an Admin can't change their own approved week' plants the approved state by hand: `update time.week set status = 'approved', locked_at = now()`. It doesn't go through submitWeek and then approveWeek by another approver. That skips the real lock path, including any approval rows or fields the lock check may depend on. It is also the only case: there is no table of variants (for example, an Admin adding time to their own approved week through MCP as agent time, or through an explicit `userId` equal to their own). Fix: have maya submit and sahan approve through the services, then run the self-change variants in a table.

The Temporal hook now runs after the control has committed and been audited. If handle.cancel() or the pause signal throws (Temporal unreachable, a connection blip), the row already says 'cancelled' or 'paused', but the Temporal execution keeps running steps. Nothing retries it: only 'retry' has a recovery path (launched_at = null plus claim_launches). This is the previous B6 fixed for start/retry only. Fix: record a pending engine action (for example a control_pending column claimed by the tick, like launches) and retry it until Temporal confirms. Or only commit the status after the Temporal call succeeds.

Temporal signal() only targets runs with launched_at IS NOT NULL. A run started inside a caller's transaction is only launched by the next tick, up to a minute later. Any event in that window is dropped on Temporal. Postgres buffers every signal since the run started, so the early-event disagreement between engines (previous B1) is back for the tx start path. The new conformance case starts without tx, so it does not catch this. Fix: also target unlaunched runs by buffering the signal in workflows.signal and seeding it into RunArgs at launch (for example, launch() reads signals created since run.created_at for the waitsFor events). Add the tx-start case to the conformance suite.

heartbeat() treats a failed renewal as success (`.catch(() => true)`). 'Could not ask' reads as 'still holds the lease'. While renewals fail, the lease silently expires, another worker claims the run, and both execute the step. The heartbeat that was added to stop exactly that is defeated. Fix: count consecutive failures and abort the step (stop.abort) once the time since the last successful renewal approaches leaseSeconds.

Per-schedule isolation covers only start(). nextFire(def.cron, row.timezone) is computed before the try. A bad zone (workflows.entity_zone.timezone is free text with no validation) or a bad cron throws out of the loop. scheduleTick swallows the error, but every later row in the claimed batch stays locked and unfired. The bad row keeps next_run_at null, so `order by next_run_at nulls first` claims it first again on every tick. Fix: move nextFire inside the try (on failure record last_error and release the lock), and validate entity_zone.timezone against pg_timezone_names (CHECK or trigger).

The zone fix is partial. A country default is still guessed for any AU entity: ENTITY_ZONES AU → Australia/Sydney. An entity in Perth, Brisbane or Adelaide without an entity_zone row silently runs its '06:00' job at Sydney time, with no flag. The previous finding asked for the zone to come from the entity rather than a country map. Fix: only default countries with a single zone (LK), and leave multi-zone countries null (not fired, flagged) until an entity_zone row exists.

workflows.entity_zone has its own tenant_id plus an FK to core.legal_entity(id). The FK does not tie the two together, and FK checks bypass RLS. ensure_schedules (SECURITY DEFINER, cross-tenant) joins `z.legal_entity_id = e.id` without `z.tenant_id = e.tenant_id`. amax_app can insert rows, so a tenant can plant a zone row for another tenant's legal entity id, and ensure_schedules then applies it to that tenant's schedules. Fix: use a composite FK (legal_entity_id, tenant_id) → core.legal_entity(id, tenant_id), and add the tenant equality to the join.

The periods are now derived from the entries, but the columns are still written twice. The entries declare start.at ['finished_at'] / ['run_finished_at'] / ['created_at'], and the job passes the same column names as hand-typed strings. `due` ignores its `e` argument. If an entry's start column changes, the job keeps pruning on the old one. Fix: take the column from e.start.at[0] (and use 'updated_at' only as idle's documented basis) inside due().

Several majors claimed fixed ship without a variant test that drives the real path and fails without the fix: (a) a step running longer than leaseSeconds is heartbeated and not re-claimed by a second worker, and is aborted when fencing is lost; (b) the tick releases claimed runs past the deadline instead of driving them; (c) a Temporal start inside a caller tx that rolls back launches nothing, and mark() refuses a missing row; (d) the Temporal connector reconnects after a failed connect; (e) retention keeps the steps of active runs and deletes them after run_finished_at. Add a test for each, with at least the named case plus two variants (for (a), use a small leaseSeconds and two engines).

The Temporal worker builds its own runtime and registry instead of sharing the web app's setup. It calls workflowRegistry([platformWorkflows, ...modules]) over every generated module, while the web app uses workflowsRegistry() over `installed`. It also only calls configureRuntime, and skips the installAuthorizer / setGrants / setViewerScopeResolvers boot that lib/server.ts does. The two copies can disagree: a module disabled via AMAX_MODULES_DISABLED still has its workflows hosted by the worker. Services that steps call run without the app's authoriser, grants and scopes on Temporal, but with them on Postgres. Fix: extract one shared bootstrap (runtime, authoriser, grants, registry) used by both lib/server.ts and the worker.

[design] scheduleTick catches any failure in syncSchedules or fireSchedules and returns 0. The tick result then reads 'schedulesFired: 0', the same as 'nothing was due'. A sync failure happens before any row is claimed, so no last_error is set either, and the Schedules card keeps showing the last good state. Fix: return the failure in WorkflowTickResult, for example `schedulesError` or `schedulesFired: null`, so /api/jobs/tick and the UI report that the scheduler did not run.

The pending-control fix (previous B6) only works for runs that are already launched. A pause or cancel on a Temporal run with launched_at IS NULL leaves engine_action set: the hook's signal() throws WorkflowNotFoundError, and when Temporal is unreachable cancel() throws too. claim_temporal then claims the row because engine_action is not null. tick() checks `!r.launched_at` first and calls launch(). launch() never looks at status, so it starts a paused or cancelled run on Temporal unpaused, and steps run before a later tick applies the action. Fix: launch() should refuse to start a run whose status is not 'running'. Settle engine_action for an unlaunched run locally: clear it for cancel and pause, and pass the paused state to the execution as RunArgs if it is launched later. Add these cases to the conformance suite.

Events that arrive before launch are only delivered on the path where workflow.start() succeeds inside launch's transaction. If start() is accepted by Temporal but the call or the commit then fails (a response timeout, a connection drop, a failed commit), launched_at stays null. Events signalled in that gap are only written to workflows.signal, because live sends need launched_at. The relaunch on the next tick gets WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStartedError and just sets launched_at, so the events buffered in the gap never reach the running execution. Postgres would deliver them. Fix: on AlreadyStarted, send the buffered signals to the existing execution as 'amax.event' (the id dedupe makes repeats harmless) before setting launched_at.

launch() seeds RunArgs.signals with every waitsFor event since run.created_at, and that includes the relaunch done by 'retry'. For a retried run, events its mirrored history already consumed are put back in the inbox with ids the workflow has not 'seen'. After history replays the first wait, a later waitForEvent on the same event can match the already-consumed event. Fix: when relaunching, leave out signals whose id is recorded in the mirrored history's wait results, or seed `seen` with those ids.

The lease-age check runs only in the catch branch. A renewal that hangs (pool exhausted, a half-open TCP connection, a lock wait) never throws before the lease expires. The 'could not ask' state then reads as 'still holding' again: stop.abort is never called, another worker claims the run, and both run the step. lastRenewed is also stamped when the query returns rather than when it was issued, which overstates how long the lease has left. Fix: on every interval, check the time since the last confirmed renewal regardless of in-flight beats, and abort once it nears leaseSeconds. Take the timestamp before issuing the query, and give the renewal a statement timeout.

Several of this round's fixes have no variant test that drives the real path: (1) a renewal that fails or hangs aborts the step (the heartbeat tests only cover renewals that succeed); (2) a Temporal pause, resume or cancel whose hook fails is left in engine_action and applied by a later tick; this is the previous B6, with no test at all; (3) a schedule whose cron or zone makes nextFire throw records last_error and does not block the rest of the claimed batch; (4) scheduleTick reports schedulesError when sync fails. The fencing-loss test plants the takeover by hand (`update ... set lease = gen_random_uuid()`) instead of a second worker claiming, and it has one case, not three. Add table-driven tests that fail without each fix.

The engine_action fix does not cover runs that Temporal has not launched yet. On a pause of an unlaunched run, apply() signals an execution that does not exist. That throws WorkflowNotFoundError, so engine_action stays 'pause'. claim_temporal then picks the row because engine_action is not null. The tick sees launched_at is null and calls launch(), which never checks status or engine_action. So a paused run is started on Temporal and runs steps. A cancel whose hook failed (Temporal unreachable) works the same way: the next tick launches a 'cancelled' run. That run executes steps until a later tick applies the cancel. Fix: launch() should start the execution only if status is 'running', or seed the pending pause into RunArgs. A cancel or pause on an unlaunched run should be settled in the database (clear engine_action, never launch). Add a test for each.

apply() accepts WorkflowNotFoundError only for cancel. Pause or resume on an execution that has already completed or failed on Temporal (it finished before the mark landed) throws every time. engine_action is then never cleared. claim_temporal does not filter on status and claims oldest first (order by created_at). These poison rows are retried forever, count in runsFailed on every tick, and take up the 50-row batch. Once there are 50 of them, no new run is ever launched. Fix: treat not-found or already-completed as settled for every action, clear engine_action when a run reaches a terminal status, and limit claim_temporal to rows that can still make progress.

The hook applies controls without the run's lease or a row lock. The tick does the same from a value it read earlier. The two can therefore send Temporal pause and resume signals out of order. apply() sends the action it was given, not the row's current desired state, and the clear is guarded per action, so the stale signal leaves nothing pending. Fix: in a transaction that locks the row (select ... for update), read engine_action and status and send the matching state. Or route every control through the claimed tick path. Add a test that runs two appliers at once.

signal() now inserts the buffer row and then sends a Temporal signal to each run inside the same DB transaction. If sending to the second run fails, the transaction rolls back and the signal row disappears, but the first run has already received the event. When no id is given, the message id is the new row's id, so the caller's retry gets a new id and the first run receives the event twice. On Postgres a failed signal commits nothing, so a retry delivers exactly once. launch() also holds the run row and the tenant-wide event locks while it awaits workflow.start. During a Temporal outage, every signal for those events in the tenant waits on the connect timeout. Fix: commit the buffer row first, then deliver after commit with the stable row id (the tick re-delivers what failed), and do not make Temporal calls while holding the event locks.

Several fixes in this round have no variant test that drives the real path: (a) a Temporal control whose hook fails stays recorded as engine_action and the tick applies it later (pause, resume, cancel); (b) a renewal that fails or hangs aborts the step before the lease expires; (c) a schedule whose zone or cron fails in nextFire records last_error and does not block the later rows in the claimed batch (the new test only checks the entity_zone trigger); (d) a sync failure comes back as schedulesError rather than schedulesFired: 0. Add a table-driven test for each, covering the named case plus two variants.

The fix decides 'was it launched' from launched_at alone. launched_at is null in exactly the gap the previous round named: Temporal accepted workflow.start() but the call or the commit failed. If a pause or cancel lands in that gap, engine_action is never recorded. claim_temporal now skips rows with launched_at null and status not 'running', and launch() returns early for those statuses. So nothing ever pauses or cancels the execution that is really running on Temporal. Fix: when launched_at is null on a Temporal run, still record the action. On the next tick, settle it against the deterministic workflow id: cancel or signal the execution, treat WorkflowNotFoundError as 'nothing to stop', then clear engine_action. In launch(), when status is not 'running', cancel any existing execution with that id instead of just returning. Add a conformance case where start() succeeds but the launch transaction rolls back, then pause and then cancel.

settle() treats any Temporal error whose text matches /already completed|not found/i as done, then clears engine_action. That pattern also matches errors where Temporal could not be asked, for example 'Namespace X is not found' or a not-found on the task queue or connection. A failure then reads as 'settled', and the pause or cancel is lost for good. Fix: accept only WorkflowNotFoundError, or the SDK's typed completed-execution error, or confirm with describe() that the execution is closed. Do not match on message text.

Still no variant test for the main previous-round fixes on launched runs: (a) a pause, resume or cancel whose hook fails stays in engine_action and a later tick applies it; (b) pause or resume on an execution that already closed is settled and stops occupying the claim_temporal batch. The new test covers only runs that were never launched, where apply() now returns early. Add a table-driven test that makes the Temporal call fail for each action and then ticks.

The row lock in apply() claims to stop a hook and a tick from sending pause and resume out of order, but no test runs two appliers at once. The lease-loss case in heartbeat.test.ts still fakes the takeover: a stub tx returns []. No second worker claims the run. Add a race test that runs a concurrent hook and tick (pause, then resume) and asserts the final Temporal pause state. Add a two-worker test where worker B really claims a run after A's lease lapses.

The 'lease another worker took' case mocks the database and fakes the takeover by having the update return zero rows. It matches the SQL by JSON-stringifying the drizzle object. The fencing-loss test in concurrency.test.ts is unchanged: it still plants the takeover with `update ... set lease = gen_random_uuid()` and has only one case. Neither drives a real second worker claiming the expired run. Fix: let a lease expire and have a second worker claim through claim_runs, then assert the first worker's heartbeat aborts. Cover at least three variants.

apply() now takes a row lock and sends the row's current state, which fixes the hook-vs-tick ordering. No test runs two appliers (hook and tick) at the same time, so the test stays green with the FOR UPDATE removed. There is also still no test where a launched run's pause, resume or cancel hook fails (Temporal unreachable), the action stays in engine_action, and a later tick applies it (previous B2 item a/2). Add a two-worker race test plus a table-driven hook-failure test over pause, resume and cancel.

This only fixes the named cases. leaks() checks strings, Secret instances, own enumerable keys and values, Map, Set and typed arrays. Everything else passes as clean: functions and closures (`typeof value !== "object"` returns false), non-enumerable properties (Error.message and Error.cause), private `#fields`, getters on the prototype, a bare ArrayBuffer (not a view, so it has no enumerable keys), and Promises. Fix: reject any function result. Walk Error message, cause and name. Treat ArrayBuffer like a view. Refuse class instances that are not plain objects, arrays, Map, Set or Date unless they are known to be safe. Add these to the AC-2 variant table.

Two gaps in decoding encoded runs. (1) decodedHolds checks the decoded text only against the raw values, not formsOf(value). Base64 of a JSON or form body that holds the value escaped is therefore missed. (2) Each run is decoded only from its first character. ENCODED_RUN also matches '/', '_', '-' and '+', so a run that starts with a prefix whose length is not a multiple of 4 (a URL path, for example) decodes misaligned, and the value is never found. Fix: compare the decoded text against formsOf(values), and decode each run at all four start offsets (and its base64url twin). Add both cases to the AC-2 table.

This is an instance fix for the missing use permission. The finding asked for authorization scoped per connector and per caller kind. recordUse authorizes the single action 'secrets:credential:use', and the connector is not part of what the authorizer sees: the test's authorizer is (ctx, action). So any actor allowed to use one connector can decrypt every connector, including msgraph-write. Fix: authorize per connector (for example `secrets:credential:use:${connector}`, or pass the connector as the resource), and cover xero vs msgraph-write and ui vs job callers in a table-driven test.

The fix for the blocker (data key cached before commit) is proven by only one failure point: the version insert trigger. B2 requires a table over the variants, and the finding named the failure points: the version insert, the audit write, the event emit and the idempotency settle. Each of these can roll back after dataKeyFor. Make the test table-driven over those failure points. Also, the test creates trigger fail_github and never drops it, and setAuthorizer(() => true) is not reset in a finally block, so a failing assertion leaks state into later tests.

The 'uncommitted' test compares the row's xmin with pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned(), which is the top-level transaction id. When the data_key insert runs inside a subtransaction (a SAVEPOINT, such as a nested drizzle tx.transaction or a service called inside another service's run), xmin is the subtransaction's xid, not the top-level one. The row then reads as committed and the key is cached before commit, which brings back the credential-loss path. The test covers only a top-level putSecret. Fix: do not infer commit state from xid. Create the data key in its own transaction on a separate connection, commit it, then re-read and cache it. Add a test that runs putSecret under a savepoint that rolls back.

ensureDataKey writes to secrets.data_key through a raw withTenant transaction, outside defineService. That breaks the architecture.md law that every write goes through authorize → validate → write → audit → emit. Before this change the key row was written inside the audited putSecret transaction. Now a tenant's root data key is created with no audit record and no event. The permission check exists only because the putSecret wrapper happens to call authorize first, and any other caller of ensureDataKey skips it. Fix: make key creation a keyless defineService (for example 'secrets.data_key.create') that runs in its own committed transaction. That keeps the commit-first property and puts the write back in the pipeline.

Last round's defect was the savepoint case: a data key inserted inside a subtransaction read as committed and was cached before commit. The finding asked for a test that runs putSecret under a savepoint that rolls back. The new table covers only failure points in a top-level putSecret, and the old xmin-based code already passed all four of those, so the test does not fail without the fix. Add rows where putSecret runs inside an outer transaction or SAVEPOINT (a nested tx.transaction, or a service called from another service's run) that rolls back. Then assert that a later value is still readable after the cache is reset.

The checker is still not fail-closed for the types it doesn't model. (1) Non-string primitives return false: a symbol carries the value in .description, and a number or bigint carries a numeric credential. (2) The Error branch runs before the PLAIN prototype check and walks only Object.values. So Error subclasses with private #fields or prototype getters pass, and so do non-enumerable own properties such as AggregateError.errors or a defineProperty'd field. That is the same non-enumerable variant fixed for plain objects through Reflect.ownKeys, now in a second copy that disagrees with the first. Fix: treat any symbol, and any number or bigint whose string form hides to something different, as a leak. For Errors, accept only the built-in Error prototypes, walk Reflect.ownKeys, and refuse subclasses. Add these to the AC-2 table.

Encoded runs are now decoded at four offsets, but a percent-encoded base64 run is still missed. ENCODED_RUN stops at '%', so encodeURIComponent(base64(...)) splits into pieces at every %2B, %2F or %3D. If the value's encoded span crosses a '+' or '/', no piece decodes to it. This is how Basic client credentials look inside a form-encoded body or query string. Fix: before matching runs, URL-decode (and base64url-normalise) the text, or add percent-decoded text as a decoding source. Add the case to the AC-2 table.

The leak walk only covers the named cases for errors and bytes. (1) The Error branch runs before the prototype check, so any Error subclass gets through even though other class instances are refused. Only name, message, stack, cause and own enumerable values are walked. Missed: prototype getters and #private fields on subclasses (for example an HttpError that keeps the response body in #body behind `get body()`), AggregateError.errors (an own non-enumerable property), and any property added with defineProperty and enumerable:false. (2) Bytes are always read as latin1. A value stored as UTF-16 (Buffer.from(v, 'utf16le'), or a Uint16Array of char codes) becomes the value interleaved with NULs, so hide() never matches it. Fix: for Errors, walk Reflect.ownKeys and refuse any Error whose prototype is not a built-in Error prototype. Read bytes as both utf8/latin1 and utf16le. Add AggregateError, a subclass with a private field or getter, and UTF-16 bytes to the AC-2 table.

The table does not test the variant that sank the previous fix: putSecret running under a savepoint that rolls back (a nested tx.transaction, or a service called inside another service's run). All four rows are top-level failures, and the round-2 xmin check already handled those correctly. So the table stays green with this round's fix reverted and proves nothing about it. Add a row that calls putSecret inside an outer transaction or savepoint that rolls back. Then assert that a later put and use in a fresh runtime still decrypt.

The new OUTER rows never run putSecret inside the outer transaction or savepoint. Both `db.app.transaction(async () => …)` and `tx.transaction(async () => …)` drop the `tx` they are given. putSecret then runs ensureDataKey (withTenant plus defineService) and storeVersion on their own connections, from getRuntime().db, and commits them on their own. Rolling back the outer transaction or savepoint touches no row the put wrote, so the 'savepoint that rolls back' variant is never exercised. That is why the assertion passes: the value is still readable after the 'rollback'. If putSecret had really been nested, its version row would have rolled back too and the value would be gone. The table would also stay green with the round-2 xmin code restored, because no put happens inside a subtransaction. Fix: drive the real nesting path, so putSecret runs on the outer tx or a SAVEPOINT on it. Then assert the property that matters: after the rollback, a later putSecret plus useSecret in a fresh runtime (cache reset) still decrypt, and no data_key row is cached when it was never committed.

plainEntries checks the prototype, the own keys and the property descriptors, and all of these can be faked by a Proxy. Its getPrototypeOf, ownKeys and getOwnPropertyDescriptor traps (or a harmless target) can report clean plain data while its `get` trap, a closure, hands back the revealed value. The checker reads descriptor values, not the values the caller will read through `get`, so the result passes as plain JSON. Fix: refuse proxies (`util.types.isProxy`) at every level of the walk, or check and return a structuredClone/JSON round-trip of the result instead of the caller's object. Add a Proxy row to the AC-2 table.

The percent-encoding fix regresses the plain `key=value` case. ENCODED_RUN now accepts '=' anywhere in a run, not just as trailing padding. In a query string or form body, the run therefore starts at the parameter name ('auth=…', 'token=…', 'client_secret=…') rather than after the '='. decodings() only tries offsets 0–3 from the start of the run, and Node's base64/base64url decoder stops at the first '='. So when the name is 4 or more characters, every offset hits the '=' and the payload is never decoded. Before this diff '=' was allowed only at the end, so the match started right after 'auth=' and decoded at offset 0. Fix: use '=' only as trailing padding, as before (`(?:[A-Za-z0-9+/_-]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})+(?:=|%3[Dd]){0,2}`). Or split the percent-decoded text on '=' and '&' before taking offsets. Then add a table row with a misaligned payload behind a parameter name.

This only partly fixes last round's finding. The OUTER rows still drop the `tx` they are given. The test was renamed to say putSecret commits on its own connection, so the 'savepoint that rolls back' case is still never driven through the real path. The finding also asked to show that a data_key row that was never committed is not cached. The new T4 assertion does not show that. It calls dataKeyFor inside a savepoint for a tenant with no data_key row at all, so SecretsUnavailableError comes from the plain missing-key path whatever the code does with uncommitted rows. It would stay green if dataKeyFor cached a row it read inside a subtransaction (the round-2 xmin defect). Fix: inside a savepoint, insert a data_key row for T4 through the real creation path (or the owner connection on that savepoint) and call dataKeyFor(sp, T4) so it is read. Then roll the savepoint back, reset or keep the runtime, and assert that a fresh dataKeyFor/putSecret+useSecret for T4 does not return the rolled-back key. Run this as table rows (savepoint, top-level tx, outer service run).

numbersHold covers only the named case: one flat run of unquoted numbers in document order. It pulls every bare number out of the JSON text and decodes them as one sequence, so the byte form of the value gets through when (1) other numbers are interleaved between the bytes, such as an array of per-byte objects or index/byte pairs; (2) the codes are quoted strings (`["97","98",…]`), because the lookbehind needs `:`/`[`/`,` right before the digits and a quote is there; (3) the codes sit inside a string (`"97 98 99 …"` or `"97,98,…"` with no closing bracket after each one). Fix: decode each array or object of numbers on its own, and include numeric strings. Or walk the parsed copy and check every number array/typed-array form against the value. Add table rows for each of these cases.

There are now two definitions of 'this text reveals the value'. Results are checked with `reveals` (hide plus numbersHold), but scrubError still checks error text with `hide` alone. So the byte-list decoding added in this diff never runs on the error path, and the two checks disagree: a byte list in a result is refused, while the same list in a thrown error's message or body goes out as is. Fix: have scrubError (and every other caller of hide used as a detector) use the same detector as checkedCopy, and redact number-encoded runs as well.

checkedCopy now quietly changes any result that is not plain JSON and returns it as `T` through a cast. Before this diff those results were refused. Map and Set become `{}`, a Date becomes a string, `undefined` fields and functions are dropped, NaN and Infinity become null, a typed array becomes an object with index keys, and class instances lose their prototype. The caller gets data that does not match its declared type and is not told. Results JSON.stringify can't handle (BigInt, cycles) are now reported as a SecretLeakError whose new message says the credential 'was about to leave', which is wrong for those results. Fix: fail closed. Refuse a result whose JSON round-trip is not structurally equal to what was given (or check with a replacer that every value is a primitive, array or plain object), keep returning the parsed copy, and use a distinct error or message for 'result not checkable'.

Resuming now depends on noteClaimProject committing in its own transaction after delivery's create has committed. If the process dies, times out, or the note's transaction fails between those two steps, the project exists but the claim has no claim_project_id. That gap is the 'created, then the link failed' case the resume path exists for. After it, a retry with the same key gets claim.projectId = null, finds `existing`, and is refused with 'choose another key'. A retry with another key is refused by claimPromotion with 'promote it with that key to finish'. The opportunity can never be promoted, and the project is orphaned. Fix: write the claim's project id where delivery creates the project. One way is to pass the claim token to delivery's create, stored on the project, so a resume can match on it. Another is to reserve the id before the create (generate the uuid in claimPromotion and have delivery create the project with that id).

stillClaimed is check-then-act in a separate read transaction, so the lease is still not enforced against the create. The round-2 finding named a create slower than CLAIM_SECONDS, and that case still orphans a project. Attempt A passes stillClaimed and calls create. While that create runs, 120 s pass. Attempt B with another key finds no claim_project_id and no project under A's key yet, so it takes the claim. A's create then commits, noteClaimProject fails the token check, and A's project is left orphaned. Fix: make the create conditional on the claim in the same transaction. Otherwise, when noteClaimProject refuses, have the losing attempt void the project it just made through delivery's contract.

The round-2 finding asked for a race test with a create stub slower than CLAIM_SECONDS. None was added, so the stillClaimed guard and noteClaimProject's token check have no test. The resume test also leaves out two cases: the link failing after a real create inside promoteToDelivery, and a crash between create and noteClaimProject. Add table rows that run two promoteToDelivery calls with a slow or blocking create stub and claimed_at aged in between. Assert that no orphaned project is left, or that it gets voided. Also add a row whose recordPromotion really fails and then resumes.

The opportunity_project test plants the state with raw `update` SQL instead of driving promoteToDelivery or recordPromotion, and the finding asked for the resumed-claim path, which it does not cover. Both rows expect two rejections against HRI, so the test only shows that an existing holder blocks later links. It never races two new links where exactly one should win. Fix: run two promotions (sequential, concurrent, and through a resumed claim) whose create stubs return the same project id. Expect exactly one fulfilled and one rejected, and check that the test fails once the index is dropped.

Removing claim_project_id fixes the named orphan case by binding every stale claim to its key for good. That drops the variant the old code and the old test handled: a stale claim under which nothing was ever made can no longer move to another key. The claim is released only from promoteToDelivery's catch, and that release is best-effort (`.catch(logError)`). So a crash, timeout or failed release between claimPromotion and the create leaves the opportunity locked to that key, and the only way out is to create a project under it. Fix: when a stale claim's key differs, allow the takeover if `lookupKey(createKey(o.id, o.claim_key))` shows nothing was started or made under it. Do this inside the claim transaction, or have the idempotency record mark in-flight work, so the slow-create race does not come back.

The release decision is a check followed by a separate write. lookupKey reads in its own transaction, then releasePromotion runs, and nothing ties 'nothing was made' to the moment of release. If lookupKey reports a key, the claim is kept for good, even when the failure came after the create and will repeat on every replay. Examples: recordPromotion hits the opportunity_project unique index, or the client lookup fails. Every same-key retry replays the same project id and fails the same way, and every other key is refused, so the opportunity can never be promoted and nothing records it as stuck. Fix: if recordPromotion refuses a replayed project for a lasting reason, release the claim and flag the project, for example by voiding it through delivery's contract. Also make the release depend on the idempotency record inside the same transaction.

The previous finding asked for three variants of the shared-project race: sequential, concurrent, and through a resumed claim. Only the first two are here, so the resumed-claim row is missing. The test also checks only that one promotion wins. It never asserts what happens to the loser afterwards: whether its claim is released or the project flagged, and whether it can still be promoted. Add the resumed-claim row, and assert the loser's state after the race.

The release path changed from 'no project object' to 'lookupKey finds nothing'. The only release test fails before the create is ever called: delivery already has CON, so the pre-check throws. No row covers a create that delivery itself refuses or that throws, which is the case where withIdempotency has run. So nothing shows the claim is given back there, or that a different key works afterwards. The old row 'a stale claim that made nothing gives way to another key' was deleted and not replaced. Add table rows where the create stub throws (validation, forbidden, thrown before commit), each followed by a promote with another key that must succeed.

The fix for the slow-create race now depends on withIdempotency handling two creates that run at the same time under the same createKey. No test exercises that case. The 'slow first attempt' test holds attempt A at the gate before create is ever called. So A's create only starts after B has already created and linked the project, and A just gets a sequential replay. The test would stay green if withIdempotency had no handling for a create already in flight: no reservation, no lock, no unique key. Fix: block the stub inside delivery's create (after the insert, before the commit), or hold a DB lock, so both creates are in flight together. Then assert that exactly one project exists and that both attempts end with the opportunity linked to it.

createKey identifies a promotion by opportunity and key only. A retry that resumes the claim with different inputs gets back the project from the first attempt, with that attempt's billing, name and client. The new input is silently ignored and the promotion reports success. Fix: either include a fingerprint of the create input in the idempotency record and refuse a replay whose input differs, or refuse a resume whose billing differs from what the claim recorded.

This is an instance fix. Only a Postgres 23505 from recordPromotion counts as a lasting refusal. Other failures after `made = true` also come back on every replay, and they still keep the claim for good. There are three: (a) projectOf now throws when delivery's result or replay has no `key`; (b) recordPromotion refuses when the key delivery returned differs from `claim_key`, because `o.claim_key !== input.projectKey` is checked against delivery's key, not the requested one; (c) the client lookup finds no row, so `c.name` throws. In each case a same-key retry replays the same value and fails the same way. Any other key or billing is refused because the series made a project. The opportunity cannot be promoted and nothing records it as stuck. Fix: decide 'lasting' by kind of failure, not by one SQLSTATE. Treat any deterministic refusal of a replayed project as lasting (validation of delivery's result, key mismatch, missing client, unique violation). Or make recordPromotion compare against the requested key and return a typed lasting error. Add a table row for each.

This is a partial fix for the round-3 input-fingerprint finding, which named billing, name and client. The series identity (`same`) covers only key and billing. The project's name and client come from the opportunity, read again on every attempt (`opp.title`, `opp.client`). When a resume replays the series' project, any change to those is silently dropped and the promotion reports success. Fix: store a fingerprint of the whole create input (key, billing, name, client) on the claim, and treat a mismatch like a billing mismatch (end the series if it made nothing, otherwise refuse). Or refuse edits to title/client while a claim is held.

This round-3 finding is still not addressed. The rewritten slow-attempt test still holds the gate before `create` is called. So attempt A's claimKey runs only after B's endSeries has committed the cancelled marker, and A just reads the marker sequentially. Two cases have no test: a create in flight (key row inserted but not committed) while endSeries runs, which the endSeries docstring says 'waits for this, then fails'; and two same-key creates in flight together. Both tests would stay green if claimKey did not block on an uncommitted row. The same-key overtake test from round 3 was also deleted and not replaced. Fix: block inside delivery's create after its key claim and insert, before commit. Then (1) run a takeover with another key and assert it either waits and is refused, or cancels with no SLO project; and (2) run a same-key resume concurrently and assert exactly one project and both attempts linked to it.

The shared-project race now checks the loser's state, but the table still has only the sequential and concurrent rows. The resumed-claim row the previous finding asked for is still missing. Nothing drives the case where the loser's 23505 comes from a resumed claim replaying a project, which is the force-release path after a replay. Add that row: the loser made the project under its series, its link failed, the claim went stale, the retry replays and hits 23505. Assert that the claim is released and that another key then works.

The billing half of the series fix has no variant test. The test is named 'gives way to another key or billing; one that made a project doesn't', but it only checks a different key (SWA→SWB). It has no row for the same key with a different billing when the series made nothing (must take over with a new series), and none for the same key with a different billing after the series made a project (must be refused, not resumed). The 'doesn't' half is not in this test either. Make it table-driven over {other key, same key + other billing, other key + other billing} × {made nothing, made a project}.

getConversation and listConversations read `pending` but never read `chat.conversation.decided`. A confirmed or cancelled card comes back from History as open, with Add it / Cancel, or as expired. listConversations also counts decided cards older than CARD_DAYS as 'expired action'. Fix: select `decided` and map each card to its decision: confirmed, cancelled, unknown, or open only when undecided. Count only undecided cards as expired, and add a variant test for confirmed, cancelled and undecided cards.

findSchedule falls back to `all.filter(title === want).at(0)`. For per-entity schedules that share a title, it quietly picks whichever comes first, so the confirm card names a schedule without its entity and the write lands on an arbitrary one. Fix: if more than one schedule matches the title, throw an invalid_input error that lists the 'Title, Entity' labels to choose from.

`await step("ok")` sits inside the try after the tool has run. If writing the trace step fails, the catch records a second step with outcome 'error' and rethrows. A write that committed is then reported to chat or MCP as a failure, and the trace says it failed. Fix: keep only tool.run inside the try, and record the ok step outside it, so a trace-write failure can't turn a committed write into an error.

The export now puts three write-once objects one after another, with no check for objects that already exist. If a later put fails, the job's retry puts the audit object again and hits ObjectLockedError. The trace and ai-call objects for that day are then never written. Fix: skip a key that already exists with the same body (or treat ObjectLockedError on an identical body as done), and write the core.audit.export row only after all three objects are written.

policyPatch accepts any string for dataRegion, aiRegion, dbRegion, storageRegion and providerRegion. The old form only allowed REGIONS codes, and a model now fills these fields. Unknown codes are stored and shown as if valid. Fix: validate the four region fields with z.enum(Object.keys(REGIONS)).nullable().optional(), and give providerRegion its own allow-list or format check.

When the current expiry has already passed, rotate_secret quietly sets expiresAt to null, so the new credential never expires. The prompt and card say 'keep its expiry', and the hub and Expiring tickets will never flag this credential again. Fix: if the old expiry is past and no new expiresAt is given, refuse with invalid_input and ask for a new expiry.

The Settings hub's Audit card ignores whether the chains verify. It always shows an info chip and never sets `attention`, so a broken audit or trace chain doesn't come first on a hub built to lead with what needs attention. Fix: read the cached auditStatus and raise a bad-tone attention when audit.ok or trace.ok is false.

Moving revokeClient and savePolicy onto defineService fixes only the cases that were named. `append` now also writes title and pins to chat.conversation with a raw update: no audit and no permission check (AGENTS rule 5). issueCode, exchangeToken/mint and revokeToken (outside this diff) are still unaudited too. Fix: route the conversation writes through a service (or record why they are exempt), and cover every write path from the earlier finding.

confirmAction appends the immutable 'decided: confirmed' trace step before confirmCard checks for replay, cancellation, expiry or a missing secret. The trace then records a confirm that never took effect, one step per retry. Cancel, by contrast, records its step only after it succeeds. Fix: record the decided step with its real outcome (confirmed, expired, already cancelled, failed) after confirmCard settles, or put an outcome in its detail.

Each module's tool card pins `settings_overview {area:'integrations'}`. That read tool returns the hub's Integrations status card, not this module's tool list, so the pin doesn't resolve to the record shown. The Events card on /settings/audit (page.tsx) has no PinButton at all. Fix: pin a read tool that returns the module's tools (for example list_mcp_tools {module}), and add a search_audit pin with the current filter to the Events card.

This fixes only the success path. The error path still writes its trace step inside the catch with a bare `await step("denied"|"error")`. If that trace write fails, its exception replaces the tool's real error, so the caller (and the model, through chat) gets a trace-store failure instead of the forbidden/invalid_input/tool error. This is the same class as the ok-step fix: a trace-write failure changes what the caller is told. Fix: wrap the catch-path step the same way, `await step(...).catch((x) => logError(...))`, then `throw e`. Add 'tool throws + step write fails' and 'tool refuses + step write fails' rows to registry-step.test.ts.

The decided step now runs on the replay paths too, before the known outcome is returned, so a trace-write failure there turns a committed write into an error. That is exactly what the registry fix forbids. Any failure of `await decide("already_done")` hides the earlier attempt's result from the person retrying to learn it. Fix: on the already_done, already_cancelled and expired paths, record the step best-effort (catch and log), so the settled outcome is still returned or thrown. Only the `run` step can stay fail-closed before the write.

The Postgres test for the history fix plants `pending` and `decided` with a raw SQL update (setCards) instead of driving a real confirm or cancel. It never shows that the real write path leaves a decided card where History reads it. If the engine stored decisions under a different key or shape, this test would still pass. Fix: create a card through chatTurn, run confirmAction on one card and cancelAction on another, then check getConversation and listConversations. Keep the hand-planted rows only for the expired-age case.

The fix adds five outcomes, but the trace test covers only three of them: needs_secret, expired and run. `already_done` and `already_cancelled` are the replay paths, where a wrong immutable step is most likely, and nothing tests them. Every case also plants the pending card with a raw `update chat.conversation` instead of having chatTurn propose it.
